title: Smartphone-derived mobility metrics identify distinct recovery phenotypes following ACL reconstruction: associations with function, pain, and psychological health.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Recovery after anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction is typically monitored through patient-reported outcomes and periodic clinical assessments, which may not fully capture real-world functional performance. Smartphone-derived mobility data provide a passive and objective approach for evaluating daily activity and recovery.
PURPOSE: To examine associations between smartphone-derived mobility metrics and recovery outcomes in adults 3-12 months after primary ACL reconstruction and to identify distinct recovery phenotypes using mobility-based clustering.
METHODS: This cross-sectional study included 120 adults who were 3-12 months post-primary ACL reconstruction and had at least 14 days of retrospective smartphone mobility data. Mobility variables included daily step count, activity volume and intensity (e.g., active minutes and walking bout duration), sedentary behavior, and walking-related metrics. Outcomes included pain (Numeric Rating Scale [NRS]), functional status (Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score [KOOS] Pain, Activities of Daily Living, and Sport/Recreation subscales), knee-related quality of life (ACL Quality of Life questionnaire [ACL-QoL]), and psychological measures including the Pain Catastrophizing Scale (PCS), Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9), and Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 (GAD-7). Associations were evaluated using Pearson correlation and multivariable linear regression analyses. Recovery phenotypes were identified using unsupervised k-means clustering of mobility metrics.
RESULTS: Higher daily step counts were independently associated with better KOOS-ADL scores (β = 0.48, p < 0.001), higher ACL-QoL scores (β = 0.45, p < 0.001), and lower pain intensity (β = - 0.39, p = 0.001). Three recovery phenotypes emerged: a high-activity/low-pain phenotype with superior function and minimal psychological distress, a moderate-activity/moderate-pain phenotype with intermediate outcomes, and a low-activity/high-pain phenotype characterized by reduced mobility, poorer function, greater pain, and higher pain catastrophizing. Significant gradients were observed across phenotypes for pain (NRS: 1.72-5.01), function (KOOS-Pain: 88.94-62.37), and pain catastrophizing (PCS: 8.52-24.91; all p < 0.001).
CONCLUSIONS: Smartphone-derived mobility metrics were significantly associated with recovery outcomes following ACL reconstruction. Mobility-based clustering identified distinct recovery phenotypes associated with meaningful differences in pain, function, and pain catastrophizing, highlighting the potential of passive mobility monitoring to support personalized rehabilitation strategies. However, given the variability in evaluation periods and uncontrolled surgical factors, future research employing standardized, long-term follow-ups is warranted.

title: Predicting Return to Play After Achilles Tendon Injury in National Football League Players Using Machine Learning.
abstract:
UNLABELLED: BackgroundNational Football League (NFL) players frequently experience Achilles tendon (AT) injuries. However, there is mixed evidence regarding factors influencing return to play (RTP) after AT injury. The objective of this study is to develop machine learning models to predict NFL players' likelihood of RTP within 1 year of an AT tear.
HYPOTHESIS: Machine learning models can predict 1-year RTP status in NFL players following AT tear.
STUDY DESIGN: Retrospective Cohort.MethodsA retrospective review was conducted to identify NFL players who sustained unilateral AT injuries from 2004 to 2024. Player demographics and performance data were recorded. Return to play was defined as generating playing statistics. Five machine learning models were developed: logistic regression, random forest classifier, XGBoost, Gaussian naive Bayes, and K-nearest neighbors. Accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 were used to assess model performance.ResultsOne hundred seventy-six NFL players were identified with an AT injury. One hundred eight players achieved RTP within 1 year (class 1), while 63 players did not (class 0). In the full cohort, injury etiology was the most influential feature associated with 1-year RTP, followed by pre-injury performance. Among the 99 players with a confirmed AT tear, 48 players achieved RTP within 1 year (class 1), while 51 players did not (class 0). Within the confirmed-tear cohort, draft round and games started were the leading predictors of 1-year RTP, which was best predicted by random forest with a mean accuracy of 0.69, precision of 0.68, recall of 0.70, and an F1-score of 0.69 for class 0.ConclusionMachine learning models that combine clinical and performance metrics of NFL athletes demonstrated potential for predicting 1-year RTP after AT injury and identifying factors associated with RTP.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Machine learning could be integrated into clinical decision-making and prognosis to refine rehabilitation approaches in NFL players.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 3.

title: Surgical Profiles of Elite Female Athletes and Their Association with Long-Term Musculoskeletal Health: Findings from the Women's Soccer Health Study.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To describe the career and post-career surgeries in female elite-level soccer players and evaluate their association with long-term musculoskeletal health.
STUDY DESIGN: This is a cross-sectional study.
METHODS: Surgical data (the number and type of surgeries during and after the career) from an anonymous online survey was obtained from a previously published cohort of 560 retired elite women's soccer players. Correlation coefficients were used to evaluate the relationship between the number of surgeries and physical activity levels (UCLA activity scale), joint function (SANE), and physical and mental health (PROMIS-10), which were all collected on the same survey.
RESULTS: The average number of career surgeries was 1 (SD=1.6), and the average number of post-career surgeries was 0.5 (SD=1). The most common career surgery sites for women's soccer players were knee (39%), foot/ankle (12%), and leg (4%). The most common knee procedures involved ligament reconstruction, primarily of the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL), followed by meniscus and cartilage surgery. The most frequent post-career surgery sites were knee (24.0%), foot/ankle (5.1%), and leg (3.2%). Knee ligament and meniscus surgeries were equally reported. More career and post-career surgeries were associated with lower SANE knee scores (p<0.001). Lower SANE knee scores (p=0.017) were associated with lower UCLA activity levels.
CONCLUSIONS: The locations of career and post-career surgeries were similar, suggesting a possible association with long-term musculoskeletal impairment, particularly to the knee, in a cohort of mostly White collegiate former players. Having more soccer-related surgeries was associated with reduced joint function and activity levels after retirement, though the correlations were weak or moderate. These findings suggest the need for the development of preventive interventions that address the specific needs of female athletes, implementation of injury prevention programs and strategies to maximize adherence, and long-term musculoskeletal assessments of players after retirement.

title: [Disordered eating behaviors and eating disorders among athletes II.].
abstract: Over the past two and a half decades, a substantial shift has occurred in the understanding of disordered eating and eating disorders among athletes. Research has gradually moved beyond the concept of the female athlete triad towards the model of relative energy deficiency in sport (REDs), which recognizes low energy availability as a key factor affecting both athletes' health and performance. The aim of this study is to review the international literature published between 2000 and 2025 on disordered eating and eating disorders in athletes, with particular emphasis on prevalence, the contemporary interpretation of risk factors, the development of the REDs concept, and current recommendations for screening, treatment, and prevention. A thematic narrative literature review was conducted using the PubMed, ScienceDirect, and Scopus databases. Publications and professional consensus statements addressing disordered eating, eating disorders, relative energy deficiency, screening, prevention, and multidisciplinary care in athletes were included in the analysis. The reviewed literature indicates that disordered eating behaviors are considerably more prevalent than clinically diagnosed eating disorders; however, both conditions adversely affect athletes' health and performance. The evidence also confirms that low energy availability is not exclusively associated with eating disorders but may also result from an imbalance between energy intake and exercise expenditure. The introduction of the REDs model substantially expanded the earlier female athlete triad concept by highlighting the involvement of male athletes, the role of psychological factors, and the multisystem consequences of low energy availability. Current international recommendations emphasize early identification, sport-specific risk assessment, and multidisciplinary care as the cornerstones of effective prevention and treatment. Contemporary approaches to nutrition-related problems in athletes consider disordered eating, eating disorders, and relative energy deficiency as interrelated conditions. The development of standardized multidisciplinary models of care consistent with current international recommendations would be warranted in Hungary. Orv Hetil. 2026; 167(42): 1702-1709.

title: Preoperative factors associated with quadriceps strength 1 year after total knee arthroplasty: a prospective longitudinal study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Quadriceps strength is highly related to physical function following total knee arthroplasty (TKA). Preoperative factors associated with long-term postoperative strength remain insufficiently understood. The aim of this exploratory study was to investigate preoperative factors associated with normalized quadriceps strength (NQS), changes in NQS and limb symmetry index (LSI) 1 year after TKA in patients with uncomplicated recovery.
METHODS: A prospective longitudinal study was conducted. Measurements took place at three primary care rehabilitation facilities in Region Västra Götaland, Sweden. The final analysis included 39 participants aged 65 years or older who underwent elective fast-track primary TKA due to knee osteoarthritis and had an uncomplicated recovery. Preoperative factors associated with NQS in the operated limb after 1 year (n = 39), changes in NQS from preoperative testing to 1 year after TKA (n = 39), and LSI (n = 35) were analyzed in three separate exploratory multiple linear regression models. Preoperative factors included age, sex, NQS, the 6-minute walk test (6MWT), and the LSI.
RESULTS: Preoperative NQS (B = 0.72, 95% CI: 0.40 to 1.0, p < 0.001) and LSI (B = - 0.17, 95% CI: - 0.29 to - 0.037, p = 0.013) were significantly associated with NQS 1 year after TKA. LSI was the only preoperative factor significantly associated with changes in NQS (B = - 0.19, 95% CI: - 0.32 to - 0.059, p = 0.006) and LSI 1 year after TKA (B = 0.41, 95% CI: 0.15 to 0.68, p = 0.004).
CONCLUSIONS: In this selected and relatively small sample, greater normalized quadriceps strength in the operated limb and higher LSI 1 year after TKA appeared to be primarily associated with higher preoperative normalized quadriceps strength in the operated limb and higher preoperative LSI, respectively, whereas strength gains appeared to be associated with lower preoperative LSI. The findings should be considered exploratory and primarily applicable to older adults with uncomplicated recovery after TKA. Confirmation in larger studies is warranted.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: Retrospectively registered February 9, 2022 ( http://clinicaltrials.gov , ID: NCT05248815).

title: Age-Related Patterns of Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs) Symptoms and Key Performance Factors in Adolescent Biathletes.
abstract: Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs) impairs health and performance, but age-related patterns in its emergence remain unclear. This study examines RED symptoms in adolescent biathletes at season-start and their link to end-of-season performance. A national cross-sectional study including prospective performance registration recruited biathletes to complete validated questionnaires, followed by clinical interviews if eating disorders (EDs) were indicated. Athletes ≥ 18 years were invited for physical laboratory assessments. End-of-season results were retrieved from open records. Analyses were performed by elastic net regression to identify the most stable predictors of performance, which were finally included in a linear regression model. Seventy-two athletes (55% females) with mean (SD) age 17.8 (1.4) years, 13.3 (3.3) training hours/week, and representing median (min, max) tier 3.0 (2, 5) were included. Prevalence in symptoms of low energy availability (LEA) was 18%, REDs 32%, EDs 11% (20% among females), and of depression 15%. Among 28 athletes (43% female) completing laboratory assessments, 11% had low BMD and ≤ 25% had clinical metabolic markers. Symptoms of mental health issues and REDs were more common in females and the older age groups. Higher training volume and low RED severity positively predicted performance, whereas injury/illness-related training absences, cholesterol, and body fat percentage negatively affected race results. RED symptoms are common in young biathletes. Illness/injury-related training absences were frequent and linked to poorer end-of-season performance, underscoring the need for routine screening by health- and performance teams to detect and manage early symptoms of LEA, reduce RED risk, and prevent premature career termination.

title: Association between sleep difficulty and baseline concussion-like symptom burden in NCAA Division I athletes.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To examine the association between sleep difficulty and baseline concussion-like symptom burden among NCAA Division I athletes and whether sleep difficulty is associated with neurocognitive performance.
METHODS: This cross-sectional analysis included 584 NCAA Division I student-athletes. Sleep difficulty was assessed using the Athlete Sleep Screening Questionnaire Sleep Difficulty Score (SDS), and symptom burden using the 24-item SCOAT6 Symptom Evaluation. Symptom number was analyzed with multivariable negative binomial regression and symptom severity with multivariable linear regression using HC3 robust standard errors. Models adjusted for age, sex, sport type, and head-injury history. Sensitivity analyses excluded overlapping sleep-related symptoms and examined individual symptoms, symptom domains, head-injury strata, and neurocognitive outcomes.
RESULTS: Each 1-point increase in SDS was associated with greater symptom number (n = 583; IRR = 1.127, 95% CI 1.086-1.169, P < .001) and severity (n = 584; B = 1.054, 95% CI 0.688-1.419, P < .001). Associations persisted after excluding sleep disturbance and after additionally excluding fatigue/low energy and drowsiness. Twenty-one of 24 symptoms remained associated with SDS after false-discovery-rate correction. Head-injury history did not modify associations with symptom number (P = .971) or severity (P = .846). SDS was not associated with memory (B = -0.012, P = .269), executive function (B = -0.017, P = .247), or psychomotor speed (B = 0.001, P = .939).
CONCLUSIONS: Greater self-reported sleep difficulty was associated with greater baseline concussion-like symptom burden but not with assessed neurocognitive outcomes. Sleep difficulty should be considered a contextual factor when interpreting baseline concussion symptom reports.

title: Changes in Hormone Cycles and Exercise Capacity During Testosterone Therapy in a Transmasculine Triathlete: A Case Study.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: The impact of testosterone therapy on the hormone cycles, exercise capacity, and physiology of transmasculine individuals is not well understood. Existing studies report limited metrics at large time intervals between data collection points.
METHODS: High-resolution temporal data were collected from a single amateur trans male triathlete over 13 months-including one baseline month and 12 months on testosterone therapy-to characterize hormone, strength, body composition, aerobic, and training load profiles.
RESULTS: Daily urine hormone monitoring revealed that progesterone and luteinizing hormone are the clearest metrics associated with cessation of menses. After 1 yr, the participant increased lean body mass by 12%, average hand grip strength by 16%, jump height by 16%, and average knee isometric strength by 18%, but did not lose fat mass or show changes in isokinetic knee strength. Fluctuations in running fitness and maximum oxygen consumption ( V ˙ O 2 m a x ) were associated with both training and testosterone levels, with future work needed to untangle their relative contributions.
CONCLUSION: This study provides the most comprehensive characterization of the impacts of testosterone therapy on hormone cycles, exercise capacity, and physiological changes in a single person to date, as well as observations to help inform the design of larger cohort studies.

title: Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction and Mental Health: A Bidirectional Relationship.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: New-onset mental health (MH) conditions are a concern for patients undergoing anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction. Patients with pre-existing MH conditions have been observed to experience poorer postoperative outcomes.
HYPOTHESIS: Patients with pre-existing MH diagnoses would report poorer outcomes after ACL reconstruction, and non-sport-related injuries would be associated with a greater incidence of new MH diagnoses.
STUDY DESIGN: Retrospective cohort study.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 3.
METHODS: Adults undergoing ACL reconstruction between October 2016 and October 2023 at a large university-affiliated practice were included. Patients completed the Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS) Global Health and Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcomes Score (KOOS) before surgery, and at multiple postoperative timepoints. MH diagnoses included anxiety, depression, bipolar disorder, and other psychiatric conditions documented through medications, International Classification of Diseases, tenth revision codes or chart notes. Continuous and categorical variables were compared using appropriate univariate tests, and mixed-model linear regression was used to compare patient-reported outcomes over time while controlling for patient sex.
RESULTS: Out of 365 patients undergoing ACL reconstruction, 50 (13.7%) had a pre-existing MH diagnosis (mean age, 36.42; 84.0% female). Groups did not differ on any scale at baseline except PROMIS Mental Health, which was lower among patients with a pre-existing MH diagnosis (47.3 vs 53.6; P < 0.001). The MH Group reported significantly worse KOOS scores at 2 weeks postoperatively, but no differences were observed thereafter. Among 315 patients without previous history of MH disorder (mean age, 32.90; 52.7% female), 8 (2.5%) developed a new MH diagnosis at 1-year follow-up. Patients aged ≤25 years demonstrated significantly higher baseline KOOS scores than patients >25 years. Among 294 sport-related injuries and 71 non-sport-related injuries, non-sport-related injuries were associated with lower baseline KOOS and PROMIS scores, and higher incidence of new MH diagnoses (7% vs 1.6%; P = 0.02).
CONCLUSION: No differences in KOOS outcomes beyond 2 weeks were found between patients with and without a pre-existing MH condition. Furthermore, non-sport-related injuries were associated with a higher rate of new MH diagnoses.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These findings may help clinicians identify patients who could benefit from additional support during recovery.

title: Early sub-maximal quadriceps motor unit firing characteristics and six-month knee extensor strength after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction: a prospective longitudinal study.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To determine whether quadriceps motor unit firing rates measured pre-operatively and during the first three months after anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction are associated with isometric knee extensor strength at six months, and to explore the relationship between motor unit action potential (MUAP) amplitude and firing rate.
METHODS: Twenty-seven participants (15 female) underwent surface electromyography of vastus medialis and vastus lateralis during sub-maximal isometric knee extension from pre-operation to three months post-reconstruction. Six-month knee extensor MVC force was modelled using Bayesian regression and interpreted using a region of practical equivalence (ROPE; ±15 N). A secondary hierarchical analysis examined MUAP amplitude and firing rate.
RESULTS: Motor unit firing rate was not consistently associated with six-month knee extensor strength across time points and limbs. In the ACL reconstructed limb at two weeks, a 1-SD greater mean firing rate was associated with 45.8 N greater six-month strength (95% credible interval [CrI] - 18.5 to 114.6 N). Six-month strength was greater in the contralateral limb (β = 198.4 N, 95% CrI 171.6 to 225.1 N), in males (β = 184.3 N, 95% CrI 32.0 to 325.1 N), and with greater body mass (β = 119.9 N per 1-SD, 95% CrI 33.4 to 207.2 N). Greater relative MUAP amplitude was associated with lower firing rate (-3.7 Hz per 1-SD, 95% CrI -3.8 to -3.6 Hz).
CONCLUSIONS: Sub-maximal quadriceps motor unit firing rate was not consistently associated with later knee extensor strength, although a stronger positive association was suggested in the reconstructed limb at two weeks. Firing rate was strongly related to relative MUAP amplitude, and its predictive value for later strength appears limited.

title: A Narrative Review of Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction Graft Choice and Its Influence on Return to Sport.
abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) rupture is among the most common knee injuries in active individuals and can lead to persistent instability, secondary intra-articular damage, and an elevated risk of osteoarthritis. Because return to sport (RTS) is a major goal for most active patients and graft selection remains one of the most debated aspects of ACL reconstruction, this narrative review summarizes the contemporary evidence on how graft choice influences RTS, focusing on the four most common grafts: bone-patellar tendon-bone (BTB), hamstring tendon (HT), quadriceps tendon (QT), and allograft.
RECENT FINDINGS: RTS rates range from ~ 65% to 73% at three years and are higher (83-90%) in elite and high-school athletes. In young, active patients, autografts are associated with higher RTS and lower revision rates than allografts, and high-level evidence-including randomized-trial meta-analyses-has not established the superiority of any single autograft. BTB offers reliable bone-to-bone healing and low revision rates; HT reduces donor-site morbidity and anterior knee pain but has variable diameter and possible flexion weakness; and QT is a versatile option with favorable biomechanics, low donor-site morbidity, and encouraging RTS data, including in skeletally immature athletes. RTS is one of several important outcomes after ACL reconstruction, alongside long-term joint health and reinjury prevention. For RTS, the literature supports autograft over allograft in young, active patients while identifying no universally superior autograft. Graft selection should be individualized to patient age, sport, activity level, anatomy, and reinjury risk; the senior author favors QT or BTB autografts for high-demand athletes.

title: Calf Injuries: Anatomy, Pathology, and Treatment.
abstract: Calf injuries are common in athletes and typically result in missed time from sport and activities of daily living. The three individual triceps surae muscles can be injured, with differing described mechanisms. Gastrocnemius or plantaris strains tend to occur during sudden explosive movement of the ankle from a dorsiflexed to a plantarflexed position with the knee in extension. Soleus strains typically occur from repetitive dorsiflexion of the ankle with the knee flexed. Imaging modalities such as magnetic resonance imaging and ultrasonography can be helpful in determining the location and grade of injury, which can aid in treatment and return to play timelines. Classically, these injuries have been graded as grade I, II, or III, with grade I having <10% muscle fiber disruption, grade II having >10 to 50% muscle fiber disruption, and grade III having 50 to 100% muscle fiber disruption. The mainstay of treatment for most calf strains is nonsurgical, with surgical management being rare but reported in the literature for isolated grade III ruptures of the medial head of the gastrocnemius. Return to sport and activities requires a graduated physical therapy program focused on restoring tissue length without excessive strain. Recent limited evidence has shown promising results with quicker return to activities and decreased pain with platelet-rich plasma injections.

title: Autologous Peripheral Blood-Derived Stem Cells Combined with Platelet-Rich Plasma is Associated With Clinical and Radiological Improvement in Anterior Cruciate Ligament Ruptures-Preliminary Clinical and MRI Findings in 47 Consecutive Patients.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) ruptures are common injuries in young and active individuals and can lead to long-term functional impairment and early onset osteoarthritis. While ACL reconstruction remains the standard of care, recent evidence suggests that spontaneous healing may be possible in selected cases. Regenerative and biologic treatment concepts have therefore gained increasing interest. This study investigates the clinical and radiological outcomes of a stem cell-based regenerative treatment for traumatic ACL ruptures and presents findings as preliminary observational evidence.
METHODS: In this single-center retrospective case series, 47 patients with isolated partial and complete traumatic anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) ruptures were treated using a biologic, non-surgical protocol. Diagnosis of an ACL rupture was confirmed by standardized clinical examination (Lachman test, anterior drawer test, and pivot shift test) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), which was additionally used to assess rupture morphology and synovial sheath integrity. All patients underwent an ultrasound-guided injection of autologous biologic products derived from peripheral venous blood, consisting of 8 mL of an autologous blood-derived stem cell preparation (BSC), comprising approximately 2-3 mL of concentrated mononuclear cells suspended in 6 mL of autologous platelet-containing plasma, injected directly into the torn ACL. Patients were allowed immediate full weight-bearing without bracing and followed a standardized physiotherapy program. Clinical follow-up was conducted for 12 months, including assessment of pain (VAS), functional outcomes (IKDC, Lysholm), return-to-sport timelines, and MRI-based evaluation of ligament morphology.
RESULTS: The mean age of the cohort was 28.1 years (95% CI 26.0-30.2). Functional outcomes improved continuously throughout follow-up, with mean IKDC and Lysholm scores of 93.6 (95% CI 92.4-94.8) and 94.0 (95% CI 92.7-95.3), respectively, at 12 months. Pain levels decreased markedly, reaching a mean VAS score of 0.36 (95% CI 0.19-0.53). Patients returned to running after a mean of 2.19 weeks (95% CI 1.93-2.45), and most resumed their pre-injury activity level by one year. No infections or re-ruptures occurred and only one secondary ACL reconstruction was recorded. Patients with an intact synovial sheath demonstrated faster return to pivoting sports (26.8 vs. 33.2 weeks) compared with patients with a complete ACL rupture. MRI at 3 months showed evidence of improved ligament morphology in all but one patient.
CONCLUSIONS: This preliminary case series suggests that stem cell-based biologic stimulation may be associated with functional recovery and radiological improvement in selected patients with ACL ruptures. Prospective controlled trials are required to validate these findings.

title: Platelet-related extracellular vesicles: Therapeutic roles in musculoskeletal disorders.
abstract: Musculoskeletal disorders are a major cause of pain, disability, and loss of function. Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) has been widely investigated for musculoskeletal repair, and interest has increasingly extended to extracellular vesicle (EV) preparations obtained from platelet-related starting materials. These include EV-enriched preparations collected from isolated platelets or defined platelet concentrates (P-EVs), from PRP (PRP-EVs), and from platelet lysate (PL-EVs). They do not represent the same biological product. Their cellular contributors, co-isolated soluble components, and molecular composition can differ substantially, and the name of the starting material does not prove the origin of every vesicle in the preparation. Preclinical studies nevertheless suggest that these EV preparations can influence inflammatory responses, cartilage metabolism, tendon-cell behavior, and the local repair environment. The strength of this evidence varies with the source material, separation and characterization methods, experimental model, and delivery strategy. This review examines the therapeutic evidence for platelet-related EV preparations in musculoskeletal disorders, while keeping P-EVs, PRP-EVs, PL-EVs, and plasma-derived EVs distinct and considering the methodological limitations that currently restrict comparison and clinical translation.

title: Efficacy of Apparent Diffusion Coefficient Sampling in Muscle Tears and Intersex Differences in Professional Football Players: A Cohort Study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is the gold standard for monitoring the evolution of muscle injuries in athletes, although no established quantitative measure of recovery currently exists.
HYPOTHESIS: Apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) values may provide a quantitative measure of muscle healing, and sex-related differences may exist in the evolution of muscle injuries.
STUDY DESIGN: Single-center retrospective observational cohort study.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 2a.
METHODS: Twenty-six professional football (soccer) players (13 male ,13 female) undergoing MRI for muscle injury were retrospectively selected between October 2020 and June 2024. All athletes underwent MRI at baseline (T0) and at 2-week follow-up, including diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) acquisitions with b values of 0-100-800 s/mm². Two musculoskeletal radiologists measured ADC values within the index lesions at each examination. Changes in ADC between the two time points (ΔADC) were assessed using a paired-samples t test, while sex-related differences were evaluated using the Mann-Whitney U test.
RESULTS: The overall mean ADC value at the lesion site decreased from 2.06 ± 0.35 mm2/s at T0 to 1.61 ± 0.30 mm2/s at follow-up corresponding to a mean ΔADC of 0.44 ± 0.20 and a 21.84% reduction. The difference between T0 and follow-up was statistically significant (t = 8.12; P < 0.001). Mean ΔADC values were 0.32 ± 0.20 mm²/s in male players and 0.56 ± 0.25 mm²/s in female players, respectively, with a statistically significant difference between sexes (z = -2.95; P = 0.003). When only hamstring injuries were considered, female players showed a significantly greater decrease in ADC over time than male players (Mann-Whitney U test; exact P = 0.02), with mean ΔADC values of 0.56 ± 0.30 and 0.26 ± 0.08 mm²/s, respectively.
CONCLUSION: Muscle injury is associated with an acute increase in ADC values followed by a progressive decrease during healing. ADC may therefore represent a quantitative imaging biomarker for monitoring muscle recovery.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: ADC measurement within muscle tears may provide a quantitative assessment of healing status and support individualized rehabilitation strategies in athletes. Sex-related differences may exist in injury pathophysiology and recovery patterns relevant to safe return to play.

title: Effects of Fatigue on Peak and Angle-Specific Hamstring-to-Quadriceps Ratios in Collegiate Women Lacrosse Athletes.
abstract: Background: Hamstring strains and anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tears commonly occur in court and field sport athletes, with prevalence being higher in females. The likelihood of such injuries has been related to the hamstring-to-quadriceps (H:Q) strength ratio. Such a ratio can be affected by fatigue, to which athletes are frequently exposed. The aim of the current study was to investigate effects of fatigue on peak torque and angle-specific functional H:Q ratios at different angular velocities, as well as the association between resting functional H:Q ratios and those obtained following fatigue. Methods: A total of 18 collegiate women lacrosse players executed maximal knee concentric and eccentric contractions at angular velocities of 60, 180, and 240°/s following a supervised fatigue protocol. The isokinetic testing was then replicated. Results: There was a significant difference in functional peak torque H:Q ratios (p = 0.021-0.041) and ratios at 60 (p = 0.013-0.044), but not 20 degrees of knee flexion before and after fatigue at all three angular velocities. No main effects of angular velocity or ratio type were observed on H:Q ratio difference. The relationship between resting and fatigued functional H:Q ratios ranged from moderate to strong across all three angular velocities. Conclusions: Fatigue was associated with reductions in functional H:Q ratios, indicating altered knee flexor-extensor strength balance under fatigued conditions. In time-constrained settings, baseline functional H:Q ratio may provide practitioners with useful preliminary information regarding an athlete's potential susceptibility to lower-limb injury after fatigue.

title: Associations of cardiac autonomic modulation and urinary adrenal hormones with marathon finishing time in middle-aged male athletes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The autonomic nervous and endocrine systems are involved in the physiological adaptation to exercise, and in experimental settings both the sympathovagal balance and the adrenal function are associated with athletic performance. In this real-life field study, the association between non-invasive markers of cardiac autonomic modulation, urinary adrenal hormone levels, and marathon finishing time in middle-aged Caucasian male athletes was investigated.
METHODS: A prospective study was conducted in male marathon runners aged ≥30 years. Continuous single-lead electrocardiographic (ECG) recordings were obtained using a wearable chest device from the day before the marathon until after its completion. Urinary adrenal hormone levels were measured before and after the race. Univariate linear regression analyses were performed to correlate general characteristics, nocturnal heart rate variability (HRV) parameters, and hormonal parameters with marathon finishing time. A multivariable model was then applied including age, body mass index (BMI), and training hours.
RESULTS: 104 athletes were enrolled in the study and 73 (median age 48 years, interquartile range = 16) had adequate data quality for the final analysis. Several HRV parameters correlated with better performance at univariate analysis; lower minimum nocturnal heart rate and vagal predominance, expressed as higher 2 Like Variations (2LV) values remained independently associated with shorter finishing time. Among hormonal variables, the post-/pre-race ratio of urinary normetanephrine hourly output and cortisol/cortisone ratio remained significant at multivariable analysis. Only BMI, but not age and training history, remained significant in a model integrating HRV and hormones.
CONCLUSIONS: Under real-world marathon conditions, specific HRV indices and endocrine markers showed promising value as indicators of physiological readiness with endurance exercise in male master athletes.

title: Isometric Strength, Joint Mobility, and Muscle Strength Ratios Among Female Artistic Swimmers from the Spanish National Artistic Swimming Team: A Cross-Sectional Study Across Age Categories.
abstract: Background and Objectives: Artistic swimming demands high levels of strength, joint mobility, and body control; however, the physical profiles of elite athletes in this sport remain insufficiently characterized. This study aimed to characterize and compare isometric strength, joint mobility, inter-limb differences, and muscle strength ratios across the Youth, Junior, and Senior age categories of the Spanish National Artistic Swimming Team. Methods: This cross-sectional observational study included 36 elite female artistic swimmers, defined by their selection for the Spanish National Artistic Swimming Team: 11 Youth, 12 Junior, and 13 Senior athletes. Anthropometric characteristics, shoulder and hip ranges of motion assessed using photographic goniometry, upper- and lower-limb isometric strength, handgrip strength, and countermovement jump height were evaluated. Age categories were compared using the Kruskal-Wallis test, followed by Dunn's post hoc comparisons with Holm correction. Inter-limb differences were analyzed using the Wilcoxon test. Results: Senior athletes generally exhibited greater isometric strength than younger age categories. Among the main between-category differences, Senior athletes showed greater normalized shoulder internal-rotation strength than Youth athletes (1.56 vs. 0.95 N/kg; group-specific 95% CIs around the means: 1.43-1.69 and 0.80-1.11, respectively) and greater hip-abduction strength (2.34 vs. 1.71 N/kg; group-specific 95% CIs around the means: 2.07-2.60 and 1.51-1.93, respectively). The corresponding omnibus Kruskal-Wallis effect sizes were η2 = 0.40 and η2 = 0.32, respectively. Differences were observed in CMJ height and absolute right handgrip strength. No significant differences were observed after normalizing handgrip strength to body mass. Between-category differences were observed in certain measures of hip mobility but not in shoulder mobility. Inter-limb differences were limited to specific variables. Conclusions: These findings provide a preliminary descriptive characterization of elite female artistic swimmers and reveal differences between age categories, primarily in specific strength variables. These cross-sectional differences between age categories should not be interpreted as evidence of developmental adaptations or training-induced changes. Given the cross-sectional design and small group sizes, the application of these findings to athlete monitoring, training, or the interpretation of inter-limb differences requires confirmation in longitudinal studies.

title: Recovery of Pre-symptomatic Tegner Activity Level After Double-Level Osteotomy for Medial Compartment Osteoarthritis: Outcomes at 24 Months.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Double-level osteotomy (DLO) provides high return-to-sport rates, but these are generally based on the immediate preoperative activity level, which may already be reduced by knee pain. We evaluated recovery to a recalled pre-symptomatic activity level and associated factors.
HYPOTHESIS: Recovery would be less frequent against the pre-symptomatic reference than the immediate preoperative level.
PATIENTS AND METHODS: This retrospective study included 51 DLO patients wishing to resume sports, with symptom durations below five years. Tegner activity scale (TAS) scores were recalled for five years before surgery and assessed immediately preoperatively and at 12 and 24 months. Exploratory Firth logistic regression included age, BMI, Kellgren-Lawrence grade, and preoperative Pain Catastrophizing Scale (PCS) to examine failure to recover the five-year TAS at 24 months.
RESULTS: Median [IQR] TAS was 5 [4-8] at the five-year reference, 3 [1-5] preoperatively, 4 [2-5] at 12 months, and 4 [3-7] at 24 months. At 24 months, 56.9% recovered the five-year TAS versus 88.2% recovering the preoperative TAS. Higher PCS was associated with failure to recover the five-year TAS (adjusted OR per point, 1.066; 95% CI, 1.008-1.143; p = 0.025).
DISCUSSION: Recovery proportions differed by reference, with interpretation limited by recall bias and patient selection. Higher PCS was associated with non-recovery in exploratory analysis.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: III; retrospective cohort study.

title: Athletes and Medical Staff in Elite Contact Sports: a Quantitative Analysis of Use, Knowledge, and Attitudes Regarding Cannabinoids.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Cannabis use among elite contact sport athletes increases with legal reform and commercial availability. Limited education in cannabinoid pharmacology, use, and risk persists among athletes and medical staff, fostering stigma and reducing evidence-based guidance and communication.
HYPOTHESIS: Athletes use cannabis but perceive stigma and discomfort discussing cannabis with medical staff.
STUDY DESIGN: Quantitative, descriptive cross-sectional surveys.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 4.
METHODS: Two anonymous online surveys were administered to elite and professional contact sport athletes (Canada, United States, Australia) and medical and training staff (February 2023 to July 2024). Descriptive statistics assessed demographics, use patterns, knowledge, education needs, attitudes, stigma, communication, and league policies.
RESULTS: A total of 166 athletes (89.7% male, 35.2% aged 18-23 years) and 64 medical staff (physicians, athletic therapists, strength and conditioning coaches, etc) responded. Knowledge (pharmacology, interactions, dosing) was low. Overall, 56% of athletes currently used cannabinoids (81% having ever used), but only 21.7% knew the endocannabinoid system and 67.4% were unfamiliar with therapeutic dosing. Among medical staff, 59.5% were unfamiliar with mechanisms, only 14% were familiar with dosing protocols, and 71.4% lacked confidence in making treatment plans. Of the athletes, 86.5% believed cannabis had therapeutic value, 72.3% wanted education, and 74.1% favored qualified scientists as instructors. Of the medical staff, 79.5% reported strong educational need, with 100% of staff desiring athlete-specific cannabinoid education. Stigma and communication barriers were substantial: 81.3% of athletes perceived public stigma, 66.1% perceived staff stigma, and only 21.4% felt comfortable discussing cannabis with medical staff. Staff believed athletes would be honest if approached; however, <50% believed athletes trusted them enough to start the conversation. Both athletes and medical staff categorized cannabinoids as supplements or medications (unlike street drugs) and both supported legalization and a revision and update on league cannabis policies.
CONCLUSION: Athletes and medical staff exhibit parallel knowledge gaps and strong educational needs amid high interest, use, and significant communication barriers. Evidence-informed education and stigma-reducing strategies are urgently needed.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Athletes increasingly use cannabinoids for pain, sleep, and recovery, while medical staff report insufficient training and low confidence. System-level education, communication, and policy updates may improve safety, decision-making, and trust.

title: Warning signs of Injury: Changes in pain, training load, and wellness in elite youth athletes.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Examine week-by-week changes during the four weeks preceding injury compared with injury-free weeks.
DESIGN: Prospective study.
SETTING: and main outcome: Training load was calculated as (weekly training minutes x average weekly rate of perceived exertion)/1000 (sRPE). Pain was assessed with a rating scale 0-10. Wellness (sleep, fatigue, stress and mental recovery) were standardized using Z-scores. Injury was self-reported.
PARTICIPANTS: Elite youth athletes.
RESULTS: Among 146 athletes, 118 (80.8%) reported 125 injuries. Mean age was 17.0 (SD 0.8). Compared with injury-free weeks, significantly higher pain scores were observed one (md [IQR]: 2.0 [0.0-4.0], p = 0.039) and two weeks (2.0 [1.0-3.0], p = 0.047) prior to injury. Median sRPE was significantly lower three (md [IQR]: 2.30 [0.75-4.20], p = 0.012) and four weeks (2.40 [0.96-3.96], p = 0.011). Sleep, stress and total wellness were significantly lower one week (mean [SD]: -0.348 [1.1], p = 0.004; -0.272 [0.9], p = 0.017; -0.244 [1.0], p = 0.011), while stress also showed reduction two weeks prior to injury (-0.244 [1.0], p = 0.042).
CONCLUSION: Changes were observed mainly in the week preceding injury. Increased pain and reduced wellness may serve as early warning signs, while decreased training load may reflect adaptation rather than causation. These findings support injury as a progressive process with detectable warning signs.

title: Is Better Diet Quality Linked to Better Competitive Functioning? An Integrative Multi-Analytic Study of Sleep Difficulty and Subjective Vitality Among Chinese Collegiate Athletes.
abstract: Background: Diet quality may be associated with recovery-related experiences and self-reported physical and psychological functioning in athletes. However, the roles of sleep difficulty and subjective vitality in these associations, together with their item-level network structure and predictive relevance, have not been examined within an integrated analytical framework. This study investigated the associations of diet quality with self-rated physical fitness and competitive psychological readiness among collegiate athletes and examined cross-sectional indirect associations involving sleep difficulty and subjective vitality. Methods: A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 1641 collegiate athletes participating in provincial-level university sporting events in Yunnan and Guizhou, China. Assessments were completed on the athletes' competition check-in day. All core variables were assessed using self-report instruments, including diet quality, sleep difficulty, subjective vitality, self-rated physical fitness, and competitive psychological readiness, with the latter operationalized using mental toughness. Cross-sectional indirect associations were estimated using PROCESS Model 6. Regularized partial-correlation networks and bridge centrality analyses were used to characterize item-level conditional associations. Ridge regression and XGBoost were further applied to evaluate out-of-sample predictive performance, and SHAP values were used to quantify the relative predictive contribution of variables within the XGBoost models. Results: Higher diet quality was significantly associated with fewer sleep difficulties and with higher subjective vitality, self-rated physical fitness, and competitive psychological readiness. Significant indirect associations were observed involving sleep difficulty alone, subjective vitality alone, and the ordered sleep difficulty-subjective vitality term in both outcome models; the subjective-vitality-only estimate was the largest. Network analysis indicated that sleep-difficulty nodes were predominantly characterized by negative bridging connections, whereas subjective-vitality nodes showed primarily positive bridging connections across communities. In the predictive analyses, Ridge regression achieved holdout R2 values of 0.415 for self-rated physical fitness and 0.341 for competitive psychological readiness. In exploratory XGBoost analyses, subjective vitality showed the highest relative SHAP importance in both models. Conclusions: Diet quality was associated with self-rated physical fitness and competitive psychological readiness, operationalized using mental toughness, with additional indirect associations involving sleep difficulty and subjective vitality. These findings provide a conceptual basis for considering nutrition, sleep, and daytime vitality within an integrated athlete-support framework. Their temporal ordering and the effects of modifying these factors require longitudinal and experimental testing.

title: Silent mechanical adaptation: Passive mechanical properties of ankle-surrounding tissues in individuals with unilateral chronic ankle instability.
abstract: BackgroundChronic ankle instability (CAI) is a complex condition characterized by recurring sprains.ObjectiveOur study aimed to compare the tone, stiffness, and elasticity of the periarticular muscles, Achilles tendon (AT), and plantar fascia (PF) between the affected and non-affected limbs of individuals with unilateral CAI.MethodsThe cross-sectional study included 75 volunteers aged 18 to 45 years who had been diagnosed with CAI by a physician. Ankle instability was assessed using the Identification of Functional Ankle Instability (IdFAI). Passive mechanical properties (PMP), including frequency, stiffness, and logarithmic decrement, of the tibialis anterior (TA), peroneus longus (PL), medial and lateral gastrocnemius (MGC - LGC), AT, and PF were assessed bilaterally using the MyotonPRO. PMP were compared between sides, and relationships between IdFAI scores and PMP on the affected side were examined.ResultsThe mean age was 27.46 ± 4.23 years. Logarithmic decrement and stiffness values were higher on the affected side in the TA (p = 0.011, p = 0.027), PL (p = 0.017, p = 0.031), and PF (p = 0.020, p = 0.028) compared to the non-affected side. Logarithmic decrement was also higher in the MGC (p = 0.029) and LGC (p = 0.005). No significant difference in frequency was observed for any of these structures (p > 0.05). The AT showed no significant differences in frequency, stiffness, or logarithmic decrement between the affected and non-affected sides (p > 0.05).ConclusionsCAI is a multidimensional pathology characterized by deterioration of the PMP of the surrounding muscles and PF. These findings suggest that management of CAI should include interventions aimed at improving myofascial tissue elasticity in addition to neuromuscular rehabilitation.Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov, TRN: NCT06987435.

title: Physical examination of the cervical spine should be conducted in female athletes with a history of concussion.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Female athletes may be at increased risk of injury following sports-related concussion (SRC), even after symptom resolution. Residual cervical spine impairments have been proposed as a potential contributor; however, these have not been well characterised in female athletes. This study aimed to examine whether a history of SRC was associated with clinical assessments of the cervical spine in female athletes.
METHODS: In this cross-sectional observational study, 156 elite and pre-elite female athletes from water polo, soccer, diving, rugby-7s and cycling/BMX were recruited. History of SRC within the previous 12 months was self-reported. Assessments included questionnaires and physical examination of the cervical spine, comprising range of motion, manual examination, joint position error (JPE) and maximal isometric neck strength. Between-group differences were examined using univariable statistical analyses.
RESULTS: Athletes with a history of SRC demonstrated a higher prevalence of reduced cervical range of motion, positive findings on manual examination, increased JPE and a history of headaches or migraines compared with athletes without concussion history. No deficits in maximal isometric neck strength were observed in athletes with a history of SRC.
CONCLUSION: Cervical spine impairments were more commonly observed in female athletes with a history of SRC within the previous 12 months, including in athletes who did not report current neck pain. These findings suggest consideration of targeted cervical spine assessment beyond symptom-based screening in athletes with a concussion history. Whether identification and management of cervical spine impairments influence subsequent injury risk requires investigation in prospective and interventional studies.

title: Prevalence and predictors of in-class dozing among collegiate athletes and non-athletes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Adequate sleep is critical for recovery and performance, yet athletes often experience less sleep than non-athletes, potentially impacting their academic performance. This study investigates the prevalence and factors in-class dozing among collegiate athletes compared to non-athletes.
METHODS: This cross-sectional study surveyed 165 athletes and 92 non-athletes using an anonymous online questionnaire, focusing on sleep duration, commute times, part-time employment, and attitudes towards sleeping in class.
RESULTS: Athletes reported a higher frequency of in-class dozing (70.4%) compared to non-athletes (55.5%, P=0.009). The primary reason for in-class dozing among athletes was fatigue from sports practice, whereas non-athletes attributed it to part-time work. Logistic regression analysis revealed that athletes had a higher risk of in-class dozing (OR=2.71, 95% CI 1.42-5.16, P=0.002), and both younger age (OR=0.46, 95% CI 0.24-0.87, P=0.016) and insufficient sleep at night (OR=0.71, 95% CI 0.55-0.92, P=0.010) were associated with increased risk.
CONCLUSIONS: Both athletes and non-athletes are not obtaining adequate sleep, with athletes particularly affected by training-related fatigue possibly causing in-class dozing. Factors contributing to the likelihood of in-class dozing included younger age, inadequate nightly sleep, being an athlete, and engagement in part-time employment.

title: Baseline Performance and the 72-Hour Performance Window Following Plyometric Withdrawal in Collegiate Sprinters.
abstract: Plyometric studies emphasise pre-post change, but coaches need to know what remains after the block ends. This single-cohort study followed 26 collegiate sprinters through 12 weeks of Monday plyometric training and 4 weeks of withdrawal, without a parallel control group. During intervention, 30 m sprint time and arm-assisted countermovement jump (CMJ) height were measured at 0, 24, 48, 72, and 96 h; 0 and 72 h were retained during withdrawal. Mixed models showed large week effects for sprint, F(1, 1534) = 2272.01, partial η2 = 0.597, 95% CI [0.570, 0.622], and CMJ, F(1, 1534) = 2537.82, partial η2 = 0.623, 95% CI [0.598, 0.647]. Time-point effects were evident, but week × time-point interactions were not. Relative to 0 h, sprint was 0.0098 s slower at 24 h and 0.0057 s faster at 72 h; CMJ was 0.311 cm lower at 24 h and 0.245 cm higher at 72 h (all Tukey-adjusted p < 0.001). Linear, quadratic, and autoregressive integrated moving average (ARIMA) models were compared by rolling one-step error. ARIMA had the lowest rolling errors and provided exploratory, model-based references for weeks 13-16. During withdrawal, 1/4 sprint and 0/4 CMJ 0 h observations fell within the 95% prediction interval; mean absolute deviations were 0.0233 s and 0.794 cm. Three of four 72 - 0 h observations were within the interval for both outcomes. The 72 - 0 h series more often fell within their model-based intervals than the 0 h series, indicating different short-term patterns.

title: Use of Botanical Ingredients Relevant to Premenstrual Symptoms and Dysmenorrhea Among Elite Female Athletes: Evidence from Doping Control Forms.
abstract:
BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES: Premenstrual syndrome (PMS) and dysmenorrhea can impair training performance in female athletes. Botanical ingredients are commonly used to manage these conditions in the general population, but it is unknown whether elite female athletes do so. This study aimed to identify botanical ingredients evaluated in studies for PMS and dysmenorrhea and determine whether elite female athletes declared them on Doping Control Forms (DCFs).
METHODS: A narrative literature review was conducted to identify botanical ingredients evaluated in studies for PMS and dysmenorrhea. Then, DCFs completed during routine anti-doping testing among elite athletes in Poland (2018-2023) were analyzed for declarations of these ingredients, both directly and as components of multi-ingredient products. The proportion of DCFs containing these ingredients was compared between female (n = 4451 DCFs) and male athletes (n = 9068 DCFs; reference) using chi-squared tests.
RESULTS: The review identified 8 and 21 botanical ingredients with evidence for PMS and dysmenorrhea, respectively; of which 9 were detected in DCFs. The most commonly declared ingredients among female athletes were ginger and turmeric/curcuminoid (1.75% and 1.26%, respectively, both studied for PMS and dysmenorrhea). Chasteberry, on the other hand, with the most extensive, albeit low-confidence evidence, for PMS, was rarely declared (0.22%). Direct declaration of ginkgo, valerian, evening primrose oil, and chasteberry was significantly more common among female than male athletes (0.22% vs. 0.02%, 0.36% vs. 0.03%, 0.47% vs. 0.03%, 0.22% vs. 0.02%; adjusted p < 0.05).
CONCLUSIONS: Declarations of botanical ingredients studied for PMS and dysmenorrhea were infrequent on DCFs completed by female athletes. Because DCFs do not record the reason for use, these data cannot establish whether declarations reflected treatment of menstrual symptoms; studies assessing indication, symptom status and motivation are needed.

title: Sleep Quality and Sleep Timing in Adolescent Gymnasts: A Cross-Sectional Study.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Given the limited pediatric-specific evidence in this area, we aimed to examine the association between federated-level gymnastics participation and sleep quality and sleep timing in adolescents. The global Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) score was defined as the primary outcome, sleep-timing measures as secondary outcomes, and individual PSQI component analyses as exploratory.
METHODS: This observational, cross-sectional comparative study included adolescents aged 12 to 16 years participating in federated gymnastics and controls who did not participate in federated sports. Demographic variables included age, sex, and parental educational level, while training-related variables included weekly training duration, number of training sessions, and training schedule. Sleep quality was assessed using the PSQI, and bedtime, wake-up time, sleep duration, and sleep latency were derived from the corresponding PSQI items. Multiple linear regression models included age, sex, maternal educational level, and paternal educational level as covariates.
RESULTS: The study included 60 gymnasts and 37 controls, with baseline differences in age, sex distribution, and parental educational level between groups. Gymnasts trained a median of 12.0 hours/week (Q1-Q3: 8.25 to 20.0) over five sessions/week (Q1-Q3: 4 to 6), with a median training-session end time of 20:30 (range: 18:00 to 22:00). In adjusted analyses, gymnast status was associated with later bedtime (B=0.392 hours, 95% CI 0.043 to 0.740, p=0.028), whereas no statistically significant association was observed between study group and global PSQI score (B=0.311, 95% CI -0.720 to 1.343, p=0.550). Increasing age was associated with later bedtime (B=0.231 hours, p=0.004) and shorter sleep duration (B=-0.398 hours, 95% CI -0.560 to -0.236, p<0.001). Among gymnasts, training-session end time was not associated with global PSQI score (B=0.141, 95% CI -0.344 to 0.625, p=0.563; R²=0.006). Overall, 19/97 participants (19.6%) met the conventional PSQI >5 threshold for poor sleep quality, although an optimal adolescent-specific clinical cutoff has not been definitively established.
CONCLUSION: No statistically significant difference in adjusted global PSQI score was detected between federated adolescent gymnasts and controls. Gymnast status was associated with later bedtime. Approximately one in five participants met the conventional PSQI >5 threshold for poor sleep quality. Given the cross-sectional design, these findings should be interpreted as associations, and larger longitudinal studies incorporating objective sleep measures are warranted.

title: Acute Sodium Bicarbonate Supplementation Enhances 10-km Outdoor Track Running Performance in Recreational Female Runners.
abstract: This study investigated the effects of acute sodium bicarbonate (SB) supplementation co-ingested with a carbohydrate-rich meal on 10-km running performance and gastrointestinal symptoms in recreational female runners under field-based conditions. Twenty-one healthy women (33.6 ± 4.6 years; body mass index 20.8 ± 1.3 kg/m; maximal oxygen uptake 48.6 ± 2.0 ml·kg-1·min-1) completed two 10-km outdoor track running time trials (TTs) in a randomized, double-blind, crossover design. Participants ingested either SB (0.3 g/kg body mass [BM]) or placebo (PLA; 0.03 g/kg BM table salt), together with a standardized carbohydrate-rich meal (1.5 g/kg BM), 90 min before exercise during the same phase of the menstrual cycle. Blood pH, bicarbonate [HCO3-], and [lactate] were measured before, and 1, 3, 5, and 7 min after the TTs; performance time was recorded. Gastrointestinal symptoms were recorded at 30, 60, and 90 min after SB and PLA ingestions. Blood pH (7.47 ± 0.03 vs. 7.42 ± 0.04, p < .001) and [HCO3-] (27.7 ± 1.4 vs. 22.2 ± 1.5 mmol/L, p < .001) were higher at rest and remained elevated postexercise following SB compared with PLA (p < .05 for all time points). TT completion time improved after SB compared with PLA (3,046.1 ± 208.7 s vs. 3,078.4 ± 206.8 s; p = .011). No significant differences in gastrointestinal symptoms scores were observed between conditions (p > .05 for all). In conclusion, acute co-ingestion of 0.3 g/kg of SB with a carbohydrate-rich meal is a practical and well-tolerated strategy to achieve higher resting blood [HCO3-] and pH as well as to improve 10-km TT running performance in recreational female runners.

title: Bone Mineral Density in Physique-Focused and Non-Physique-Focused Female Collegiate Athletes: Associations With Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport Risk Factors.
abstract: Kolb, DE, Cipriano, NL, Moody, RA, Stephens, JA, Caldwell, LK, Lindley, MR, Ware, ME, and Deemer, SE. Bone mineral density in physique-focused and non-physique-focused female collegiate athletes: Associations with relative energy deficiency in sport risk factors. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-Bone mineral density (BMD) is a critical indicator of skeletal health and long-term injury risk in athletic populations. Female athletes are susceptible to changes in BMD because of sport-specific training demands, hormonal dysregulation, and energy availability. The present study aimed to compare BMD between physique-focused (PF; endurance, aesthetic, and weight-dependent sports) and non-physique-focused (NPF; ball, power, and skill-based sports) female collegiate athletes and assess risk factors associated with relative energy deficiency in sport (REDs) across both groups. Thirty-three female athletes were evaluated for BMD by dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA), REDs risk using the Clinical Assessment Tool 2 (CAT2), anthropometric measurements, blood biomarkers, the Eating Disorder Examination Questionnaire (EDE-Q), and the Low Energy Availability in Females Questionnaire (LEAF-Q). Group differences were assessed using independent t-tests with significance set at p < 0.05. Physique-focused athletes demonstrated significantly lower DXA-derived z-scores at anteroposterior spine, right and left femur, and total body sites than NPF athletes (p < 0.001). There were no differences in leptin (p = 0.35), cortisol (p = 0.16), vitamin D (p = 0.29), LEAF-Q total score (p = 0.72), or global EDE-Q score (p = 0.10). No group differences in CAT2 REDs risk were observed; thus, subjects were combined: 19 athletes were classified as "green;" 12 were "yellow;" and 2 were "orange." Lower BMD in PF athletes supports the importance of early screening and targeted interventions to support bone health. These findings suggest sport type may influence skeletal outcomes independent of traditional REDs indicators, emphasizing the need for sport-specific assessment strategies.

title: Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport and its Implications for the Foot and Ankle Surgeon.
abstract: Relative energy deficiency in sport (RED-S) is a syndrome caused by low energy availability that affects multiple physiologic systems in both male and female athletes. Stress fractures of the foot and ankle are often the first signs of RED-S; therefore, it is crucial that orthopedic surgeons are aware of and able to identify this disorder. This article focuses on RED-S and provides a framework for understanding the disorder, it's relevancy to the orthopedic foot and ankle surgeon, and offers suggestions for diagnostic strategies and treatment approaches that are imperative for safe return to play.

title: Tracking Recovery After TKA with Instrumented Timed Up and Go: Spatiotemporal, Rotational, and Strength Adaptations over Six Months.
abstract: Knee osteoarthritis (KOA) is a leading cause of disability, and total knee arthroplasty (TKA) improves pain and functional mobility, although gait impairments may persist postoperatively. This study investigated longitudinal changes in patient-reported outcomes, muscle strength, and gait performance using an instrumented Timed Up and Go (iTUG) test with wearable inertial measurement units (IMUs). Twenty-two patients with end-stage KOA were assessed preoperatively and at 3, 12, and 24 weeks postoperatively. The Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score five-subscale composite (KOOS5) showed a significant overall change over time (p < 0.001), while isometric muscle strength showed significant overall changes across all tested muscle groups (p ≤ 0.008), with mean values demonstrating an initial postoperative decline followed by subsequent increases. Total TUG duration showed a significant overall time effect (p = 0.023), with significant reductions observed in the forward and return gait phases (p = 0.012 and p = 0.001, respectively). End-turning maximum rotational speed and sit-to-stand vertical acceleration showed significant overall time effects (p = 0.012 and p = 0.024, respectively), whereas the remaining parameters did not reach statistical significance. These findings indicate that recovery following TKA is multidimensional, with significant changes in patient-reported outcomes, muscle strength, and functional mobility. iTUG analysis identified phase-specific changes, while several turning and transitional parameters did not show significant longitudinal changes, supporting the use of targeted rehabilitation strategies focusing on dynamic stability and movement control.

title: Advanced Analytics Show Domain-Specific Performance Changes After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction in National Football League Players.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To evaluate return to play, performance, and assess performance changes after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction using advanced statistics in National Football League players.
METHODS: National Football League players who underwent anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) between 2017 and 2024 were identified using publicly available databases and injury reports. Demographic and outcome data for 1 year preinjury to 2 years postinjury were obtained. Return to play was defined as being listed as active for a regular season game after injury. Return to performance was defined as returning to greater than 90% of preinjury performance. Our primary performance outcome was Sports Information Solutions points above replacement (PAR). Binary logistic regression was used to determine factors associated with return to play and return to performance. Preinjury and postinjury performance data at the first and second postinjury year were compared with paired t-tests.
RESULTS: We included 237 players in return-to-play and 173 players in return-to-performance analyses. Of players, 75.5% returned to play; players with more preinjury games played, more index games played, starters, and players with greater preinjury PAR were more likely to return to play (P = .03, P < .001, P < .001, P < .001, respectively). Fifty-one percent of players who returned to play returned to performance; younger age and players with lower preinjury PAR were significantly more likely to return to performance (P = .004, P < .001). Total PAR was significantly decreased at the postinjury year 1 and year 2 seasons (P = .002, P = .004), driven at both time points by significantly decreased rushing (P = .02, P = .001) and pass coverage (P = .003, P = .03) PAR.
CONCLUSIONS: After anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction, National Football League players with more preinjury games played and higher preinjury performance are more likely to return to play; younger players with lower preinjury performance are more likely to return to performance; and there is a significant decrease in overall performance 1 and 2 years after injury, driven by decreased rushing and pass coverage performance.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level IV, retrospective case series.

title: Editorial Commentary: Allograft Reconstruction in Chronic Proximal Hamstring Tendon Avulsions: Bridging the Gap May Not Equal a Full Return.
abstract: Proximal hamstring tendon avulsions are being treated surgically at rising rates, and although primary repair reliably restores function and return to sport in the acute setting, chronic and significantly retracted tears present a far more difficult problem. When direct repair is not feasible for a chronic, retracted proximal hamstring tendon avulsion, allograft reconstruction offers a bridge across a gap that would otherwise go unaddressed. However, significant chronicity and retraction are difficult challenges to overcome, and patient expectations must be appropriately counseled. As a salvage procedure, allograft reconstruction may improve patient outcomes significantly; however, it is not expected to restore full function, return athletic individuals to their baseline and preinjury level of sports participation, or match the success of primary repair. Allograft reconstruction may also carry more than double the risk of rerupture, which is important to discuss with patients up front. Graft choice and postoperative rehabilitation protocols remain heterogeneous across the limited available literature, and a validated tool to risk-stratify which chronic, retracted tears are best served by reconstruction versus continued nonoperative management does not yet exist. These findings suggest that allograft reconstruction is a viable and clinically meaningful option for a difficult, often nonoperatively unsalvageable problem, but surgeons should frame it for patients as a salvage procedure rather than a full restoration of function, and expectations should be set accordingly.

title: Multi-Modal Biometric Fusion for Athletic Performance Optimization: Clinical Validation of the Dynamic Multi-Sensor Fusion Classifier (DMSFC).
abstract: Integrating real-time biometric monitoring into sports science is increasingly important for optimizing athletic performance and reducing injury risk. However, many existing systems have limited capacity to accurately combine data from multiple biometric sources. This study evaluated the Dynamic Multisensor Fusion (DMSFC) classifier for analyzing physiological and functional data collected from multiple biometric modalities, including electrocardiography (ECG), fingerprint measurements, and facial recognition. A multimodal biometric framework based on DMSFC was developed to monitor and classify key health and performance indicators in elite athletes. The variables evaluated included heart rate (HR), oxygen saturation (SpO₂), blood pressure (BP), flexibility, muscle strength, and endurance capacity. The performance of the classifier was evaluated using accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). After implementing the proposed monitoring framework, improvements were observed in the evaluated performance and health indicators. The mean heart rate decreased from 78 to 66 beats per minute, while oxygen saturation slightly increased from 98% to 99%. Blood pressure decreased from 120/80 mmHg to 110/70 mmHg. Flexibility improved from 32 to 36 cm, muscle strength increased from 105 to 122 pounds, and endurance capacity increased from 20 to 24 minutes. Among the evaluated classifiers, DMSFC showed a strongest overall performance (i.e., accuracy of 0.94, sensitivity of 0.91, specificity of 0.96, and AUC of 0.97). These findings suggest that DMSFC could be capable of providing an effective framework for multimodal biometric analysis in sports science. Its use may support athlete assessment, facilitate the development of individualized training programs, and contribute to injury prevention strategies. Because the reported physiological changes were observed after implementation of the framework, further controlled studies are needed to determine whether they were caused by the monitoring system, the associated exercise program, or other factors.

title: Immediate effect of verbal cues on ACL injury relevant Knee loading during 180° and 90° cutting maneuvers in female university soccer and basketball athletes.
abstract: Young female athletes possess a high risk of rupturing their anterior cruciate ligament (ACL). High external peak knee abduction moments (pKAM) are a likely key risk factor for non-contact ACL injuries. The aim of this study was to evaluate the effect of performance-based movement feedback on pKAM during cutting maneuvers in female university athletes. Thirty-four female university soccer and basketball athletes completed preplanned 180° and 90° cutting trials while ground reaction forces and kinematics were simultaneously captured. Participants immediately received verbal cues targeting foot strike angle, foot progression angle, or trunk lean angle based on their performance. Athletes then repeated the trials post-feedback. Changes in pKAM between baseline and post-feedback trials were analyzed. Soccer and basketball athletes who received the FOOTstrike-angle cue significantly reduced pKAM for both cutting tasks (Soccer: 180°; -0.21 Nm/kg, p < 0.01, d = 0.92; 90°; -0.28 Nm/kg, p < 0.01, d = 1.16. Basketball: 180°; -0.07 Nm/kg, p = 0.02, d = 0.76; 90°; -0.30 Nm/kg, p < 0.01, d = 0.82). The FOOTpro-angle cue significantly reduced pKAM during the 180° cut for soccer athletes (-0.10 Nm/kg, p = 0.01, d = 0.60), but not basketball. The TRUNKlean cue did not significantly affect pKAM for either sport. Individual feedback targeting forefoot landings and neutral foot progression angles can elicit immediate technique change and reduce ACL injury relevant knee loading during cutting maneuvers.

title: Facilitators and Barriers to Treatment Access and Use in Black Individuals With Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury: A Qualitative Study.
abstract:
CONTEXT: Individuals with anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury are at high risk of knee osteoarthritis. Black individuals with osteoarthritis have worse pain and disability than White individuals. Racial disparities in ACL treatment use (ACL reconstruction and physical therapy) may contribute to disparities in long-term osteoarthritis-related disability. However, factors influencing ACL injury disparities are unknown. We explored facilitators and barriers to treatment access and use in Black individuals with ACL injury.
DESIGN: Qualitative (semistructured interviews).
METHODS: We included Black or African American individuals who self-reported ACL injury up to 5 years prior to recruitment, no longer seeking care for the injury, and 16-50 years old. We conducted one-on-one semistructured interviews and topics included facilitators and barriers to care, perceived communication, medical trust, and perceived discrimination. We used a reflexive thematic analysis approach to analyze the interviews.
RESULTS: We included 10 participants (age 21-49 y, 8 women). We generated 4 themes: (1) path to diagnosis, (2) patient approach to treatment, (3) patient-provider interactions, and (4) life demands. ACL injury recovery was often complex with frustrations particularly common during the diagnosis process due to lack of an accurate diagnosis and poor communication on next steps. Participants took various approaches to treatment use including active, passive, and more autonomous approaches. Family obligations and transportation barriers posed challenges to accessing treatment. Lack of health insurance was a barrier affecting multiple aspects of recovery. Participants often desired shared decision making. Several types of perceived discrimination were discussed including race, gender, insurance, and weight. Facilitators were often related to positive communication or athletic program resources.
CONCLUSION: Facilitators included shared decision making, provider empathy and encouragement, and athletic program resources. Barriers included a lack of listening to patients' concerns, lack of health insurance, transportation challenges, and perceived discrimination.

title: Do Athletes Lose Soleus Strength Over the Course of a Season? Longitudinal Monitoring of Seated Plantar Flexion Maximum Voluntary Contraction Strength and Factors That Affect It in Australian Football Players.
abstract: Green, B, Pizzari, T, Schache, AG, Rio, EK, Evans, SCS, Cooper, S, and Murphy, MC. Do athletes lose soleus strength over the course of a season? Longitudinal monitoring of seated plantar flexion maximum voluntary contraction strength and factors that affect it in Australian football players. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-The calf muscles are critical to dynamic lower-limb function in sports but are susceptible to injury. Despite its role in performance and injury, research has not evaluated soleus strength changes over the course of a season, or factors affecting it. Flexed-knee maximum plantar flexion strength was longitudinally monitored in state-league Australian footballers (2 Western Australian and 1 Victorian team) across 1-season at timepoints: preseason (T0), early in-season (T1), late in-season (T2). Generalized estimating equations evaluated strength outcomes over time (absolute, relative, asymmetry). Intrinsic factors (e.g., age, sex, injury history, sport exposure history, calf-focused resistance training) were analyzed to determine longitudinal associations with strength. Forty-one athletes (32 male, 9 female) were monitored across 210 strength measurements from T0 to T2. Absolute (T0 = 121.7 ± 27 kg; T1 = 135.2 ± 27.3 kg; T2 = 135.8 ± 25.9 kg) and relative (T0 = 1.51 ± 0.28 body mass [BM]; T1 = 1.69 ± 0.27 BM, T2 = 1.75 ± 0.26 BM) strength demonstrated longitudinal change (absolute: β = 19.33 kg, relative: β = 0.24 BM; p < 0.001). Reduced strength was associated with a recent calf injury history (relative and absolute: p < 0.001) and older age (p = 0.03). Lower strength (absolute: β = -23.53 kg, relative: β = -0.22 BM; p < 0.05) and larger asymmetry (β = 8.13 kg, p = 0.01) were detected in female athletes. Athletes can be expected to improve and maintain soleus capacity across seasonal periods. Athlete age, calf injury history, and sex can affect strength longitudinally. These findings may guide individualized prevention, performance, and postinjury benchmarking.
