title: Effects of In-Season Contrast Strength Training on Jump Performance and Sprint Ability in Female Field Hockey Players.
abstract: Chilingirian-Padrón, R, Álvarez-Yates, T, and García-García, O. Effects of in-season contrast strength training on jump performance and sprint ability in female field hockey players. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-The purpose of this study was to examine the effects of a 6-week in-season contrast strength training program incorporating sport-specific tasks on neuromuscular performance in sub-elite female field hockey players. Twenty-five athletes completed a pre-post single-cohort intervention integrated into their regular team schedule. Each session consisted of 3 sequential blocks: (a) a high-load strength exercise targeting maximal strength or hypertrophy (70-85% 1 repetition maximum [1RM]); (b) a biomechanically related explosive action performed at low load (∼30% 1RM) and high execution velocity; and (c) a high-speed sport-specific task. Jump performance was assessed using bilateral and unilateral countermovement jumps (CMJs) and free arm CMJ, whereas sprint ability was evaluated through 10- and 20-m sprints. A mixed-model repeated-measures analysis of variance was used to determine the effects of the intervention, with Time (Pre, Post) as within-subject factor and Playing Position (defenders, midfielders, forwards) as between-subject factor, with the level of significance set at p ≤ 0.05. Significant improvements were observed in all jump and sprint assessments: jump performance increased by 5.7-29.6%, whereas sprint ability improved by 1.6-1.9%. These findings indicate that 6 weeks of contrast strength training incorporating high-speed sports-specific tasks performed during the competitive season elicited meaningful improvements in stretch-shortening cycle-related jump performance and sprint ability in sub-elite female field hockey players.

title: Biceps rerouting and derotational radial osteotomy: A technique for correcting forearm supination in NBPBP.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Forearm supination deformity is a recognized late sequela of neonatal brachial plexus birth palsy (NBPBP) that can impair functional positioning of the hand and limit activities requiring forearm pronation. Surgical options include forearm osteotomy, tendon rerouting, tendon transfer, and combined procedures. We describe a modified technique combining derotational radial osteotomy with biceps tendon rerouting using cortical button fixation.
METHODS: This was a single-patient technical case report. An 18-year-old male with longstanding fixed forearm supination deformity secondary to NBPBP underwent radial derotational osteotomy and biceps tendon rerouting. The biceps tendon was detached with the forearm in maximal supination, rerouted through the interosseous space, and secured with a cortical button with the forearm in maximal pronation. A radial osteotomy was subsequently performed toward pronation with approximately 30° to 45° of rotational correction. Postoperative rehabilitation included protected immobilization followed by progressive range of motion and strengthening.
RESULTS: Preoperatively, the forearm rested in approximately 15° of supination, with active pronation limited to neutral and active supination to approximately 50°. Following surgery, the forearm rested in approximately 15° to 20° of pronation. Passive forearm rotation improved from 45° of supination to 40° of pronation preoperatively to 60° of supination to 75° of pronation postoperatively. At 12 months, active pronation improved from neutral to 55° of pronation. No postoperative complications were reported during follow-up. The patient participated in occupational therapy 1 to 2 times weekly during recovery.
CONCLUSION: This case demonstrates the technical feasibility of combining radial derotational osteotomy with biceps tendon rerouting using cortical button fixation for longstanding supination deformity following NBPBP. The technique provides an additional fixation option for tendon rerouting while addressing the underlying osseous rotational deformity. Given the single-patient design and absence of comparative or biomechanical data, further study is required to determine whether cortical button fixation offers advantages over established tendon fixation methods and to evaluate the reproducibility and clinical efficacy of this approach.

title: Arthroscopic Circumferential Labral Repair and Biceps Tenodesis in Elite Throwing Athletes: Technical Considerations.
abstract: SLAP lesions are a common cause of shoulder pain in overhead athletes and are often seen together with circumferential labral tearing, partial-thickness rotator cuff tearing, and biceps pathology. Isolated repair of the superior labrum has produced inconsistent outcomes, with low return-to-play rates in professional throwers. In patients with these complex cases, instability and anterior shoulder pain often coexist, and isolated labral repair or tenodesis may not be adequate treatment. Conversely, tenodesis without superior labral repair may increase glenohumeral translation. The senior author believes long head of the biceps tendon release reduces traction on the SLAP repair and may support healing. We describe an arthroscopic technique for circumferential labral repair, with knotless all-suture anchors performed in the beach-chair position, combined with open subpectoral biceps tenodesis and adjunct subacromial decompression. This technique restores stability, removes the biceps as a pain generator, eliminates traction on the repaired labrum, and preserves motion.

title: Extracorporeal shockwave therapy in common tendinopathies.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Extracorporeal shockwave therapy (ESWT) was initially used for urologic issues only. After Valchanou and Michailov started applying it in orthopedics in 1991, they focused on treatment of pseudarthrosis and delayed fracture healing. Some years later, shockwave therapy was also used for tendinopathies. Today, ESWT is the first-choice treatment for tendinopathies and is unsurpassed in terms of effectivity and side effects.
METHODS: This article discusses common regions of lower extremity tendinopathies (greater trochanter pain syndrome, quadriceps tendinopathy, patellar tendinopathy, Achilles tendinopathy) in a narrative review of the evidence-based literature and guidelines of leading shockwave societies such as the International Society for Medical Shockwave Treatment (ISMST) and the Deutschsprachige internationale Gesellschaft für Extrakorporale Stosswellentherapie (DIGEST). Additional case studies are also presented.
RESULTS: Extracorporeal shockwave therapy shows excellent results in the evidence-based literature and in clinical application. No other conservative treatment option in orthopedics is described as intensively in the evidence-based literature as shockwave therapy. ESWT seems to be more effective when it is accompanied by an eccentric loading/physiotherapy program.
CONCLUSION: Extracorporeal shockwave therapy enables tendon regeneration, long-term improvement, and faster return to sport, with predictable side effects and excellent tolerance.

title: Toward Wearable Joint Load Monitoring: Concurrent Estimation of Hip, Knee, and Ankle Sagittal Contact Forces from Sparse IMU Measurements.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Continuous monitoring of lower extremity joint contact forces is critical for rehabilitation medicine, sports injury prevention, and assistive device development. Yet, current wearable solutions often lack multi-joint integration or require cumbersome sensor arrays. This study aims to concurrently estimate hip, knee, and ankle sagittal compressive contact forces using a sparse inertial measurement unit (IMU) configuration across diverse daily activities.
METHODS: We collected data from 14 healthy adults equipped with four IMU sensors performing various daily movements, with reference contact forces captured using optical motion capture and force platforms. To estimate joint contact forces, we developed a domain-informed multi-task temporal convolutional network (Ada-Att-MTCN). This architecture integrates a shared temporal convolutional network encoder, task-specific attention mechanisms, homoscedastic uncertainty-based dynamic task weighting, and a soft physiological-bound penalty. Performance was evaluated using 14-fold leave-one-subject-out nested cross-validation against 4 baseline methods, with root mean square error (RMSE) and coefficient of determination (R²) as evaluation metrics.
RESULTS: On the self-collected dataset, Ada-Att-MTCN achieved the highest accuracy across all activities, with mean RMSEs of 0.328 ± 0.13 BW (hip), 0.380 ± 0.09 BW (knee), and 0.365 ± 0.15 BW (ankle), and an average R2 of 0.822 ± 0.10. On the external dataset, Ada-Att-MTCN likewise performed best among all methods (average R² = 0.754 ± 0.05).
CONCLUSION: The proposed framework captures complex inter-joint dynamics, enabling robust simultaneous load estimation with drastically reduced hardware complexity.
SIGNIFICANCE: This approach provides a practical, non-invasive solution for transitioning lab-grade multi-joint load monitoring to wearable deployment in rehabilitation and sports medicine.

title: Should athletes take omega-3 supplements? Current evidence for recovery, adaptation and performance.
abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: To evaluate whether long-chain n-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid supplementation provides meaningful benefits for recovery, training adaptation or performance in athletic populations, while distinguishing mechanistic plausibility from demonstrated functional effects.
RECENT FINDINGS: Recent data from athletic populations show that Omega-3 Index (O3I) values commonly fall below proposed cardioprotective thresholds, although athlete-specific targets remain unvalidated. Meta-analyses and controlled trials suggest that supplementation may modestly reduce muscle soreness and attenuate selected losses of muscle function following damaging exercise. However, findings are inconsistent across formulations, doses and outcomes, and benefits do not translate reliably into improved strength, endurance, power or sport performance. Evidence concerning female, masters and contact-sport athletes is limited.
SUMMARY: Routine supplementation cannot at present be recommended for all athletes. Targeted supplementation may be considered following dietary and, wherever appropriate, biomarker assessment, while recognizing that benefits during unusually damaging or congested training remain unproven.

title: Prebiotics in sport and exercise: current evidence, practical applications, and methodological considerations.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Prebiotics are selectively utilized by the host microbiota and can confer health and/or performance benefits, in part through increasing the abundance of beneficial gut microorganisms and their metabolites. While several studies have shown promising initial findings, high-quality scientific evidence examining the effects of prebiotics on athlete performance, health and wellbeing remains limited.
METHODS: This narrative review summarizes the current available evidence on prebiotic intake in athletic populations, including effects on gastrointestinal structure and function, immune responses, recovery, sleep, wellness, mood and exercise performance. In areas where there is limited evidence in athletic cohorts, but a physiological rationale for a benefit, findings from sedentary and/or clinical populations are evaluated, and the potential relevance of these findings to athletes are discussed. Finally, considerations for practitioners around the use of prebiotics with athletes are provided, and recommendations for designing future prebiotic-based research are explored.
RESULTS: Despite the limited existing literature around prebiotic use in athletes, there are several studies that indicate their potential to improve gut barrier integrity and reduce the incidence/severity of gastrointestinal symptoms. Data also indicates that prebiotics can increase salivary Immunoglobulin A secretion rate and reduce the duration and/or severity of upper respiratory symptoms in trained individuals. Other areas with emerging evidence that warrant further investigation in athletic populations include prebiotics' ability to support exercise adaptation and recovery, promote sleep improvements and enhance mood and cognitive function. The interpretation of current studies is limited by the lack of gut microbiome and metabolome measures and the absence of robust performance measures following a period of prebiotic supplementation. Well-controlled, adequately powered studies incorporating these outcomes are needed to determine the contexts in which prebiotic intake can meaningfully improve health and performance metrics, and to elucidate the underlying physiological mechanisms of any beneficial effects.
CONCLUSION: Prebiotic intake represents a promising intervention to attenuate exercise-induced disturbances to the intestinal epithelium, reduce exercise-associated gastrointestinal symptoms, and lower the duration/severity of upper respiratory symptoms in athletes. Future studies should prioritize high-quality performance assessments, alongside comprehensive microbiome and metabolome profiling, to elucidate mechanistic effects. Areas with limited current evidence such as recovery, sleep, mood, cognitive function, bone health and nutrient absorption in athlete cohorts should also be further explored.
journal: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

title: Core Muscle Injury: A Combined Orthopaedic and General Surgery Algorithmic Approach for Diagnosis, Imaging, and Treatment.
abstract: » Core muscle injury (CMI) is a common cause of groin pain in athletes and reflects pathology of the inguinal canal, rectus abdominis-adductor longus (RA-AL) aponeurosis, and pubic symphysis. » There is a substantial lack of consensus on terminology and diagnostic criteria for CMI, hindering standardized evaluation, management, and research initiatives. » Diagnosis relies on structured history, physical examinations, and provocative maneuvers to identify CMI and concurrent pathology, and fluid-sensitive pelvic magnetic resonance imaging to characterize RA-AL injury. » Treatment strategies differ across sports medicine physicians, general surgeons, and orthopaedic surgeons, underscoring the need for early cross-departmental referrals to ensure all contributing pathologies are comprehensively identified and addressed. » When both adductor/RA-AL aponeurosis and inguinal canal/abdominal wall pathologies are present, prioritizing collaborative cases between orthopaedic and general surgeons is essential for decreasing operating room time, streamlining rehabilitation, and optimizing return-to-sport outcomes.

title: Fluoroscopy-Guided Intra-Articular Hip Corticosteroid Injections: Diagnostic and Therapeutic Utility, Technique, and Steroid Selection.
abstract: Intra-articular hip corticosteroid injection is a practical option for selected patients with hip pain, particularly osteoarthritis, and may also clarify whether symptoms arise from the hip rather than the lumbar spine or periarticular structures. This review evaluates the diagnostic and therapeutic utility of injections performed under fluoroscopy, summarizes technique, and discusses steroid selection and dosing. # Recent Findings Randomized trials and contemporary syntheses support clinically meaningful short-term improvement in pain and function after image-guided hip corticosteroid injection, although durability is variable and repeated-injection data remain limited. Fluoroscopy provides continuous visualization of osseous landmarks and contrast-confirmed intra-articular spread. Ultrasound avoids radiation and may be more convenient depending on physician comfort level and ultrasound skills. Safety discussions have emphasized transient systemic effects, uncertain associations with rapidly progressive osteoarthritis, and the timing of injection before arthroplasty. # Summary Fluoroscopy-guided injection remains a reliable, reproducible diagnostic and therapeutic tool when the pain generator is uncertain or short-term symptom control may facilitate rehabilitation, bridge care, or support shared surgical decision-making. Benefit depends on careful patient selection, technically confirmed intra-articular delivery, conservative dosing, and explicit counseling that relief is usually temporary and that structural disease is not reversed.

title: Is the annular ligament disrupted in Monteggia fracture-dislocations? A cadaveric mechanistic study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Monteggia fracture-dislocation is characterized by an ulnar fracture with radial head dislocation. The mechanisms of dislocation and annular ligament integrity remain unclear. This study established a cadaveric Monteggia fracture-dislocation model to investigate radial head dislocation and associated annular ligament injury.
METHODS: Twelve upper limbs from 6 fresh-frozen cadavers (mean age at death, 83 years; 1 male, 5 females) were examined. Soft tissues were removed while preserving the bones, ligaments, capsules, forearm interosseous membrane, and biceps tendon insertions. The humeroulnar joint was fixed at 90° flexion, and the ulna was manually fractured to create a Bado type I (direct-blow) Monteggia fracture-dislocation model. The annular ligament, quadrate ligament, oblique cord (Weitbrecht ligament), and forearm interosseous membrane were evaluated.
RESULTS: Ulnar fracture created forearm deformity, causing the radius to contact the triangular fulcrum. Continued manual loading caused the radius to pivot around the fulcrum. The annular ligament remained intact in 11 of 12 limbs; 1 specimen showed injury at the annular ligament-capsular junction. In 11 limbs, the radial head was dislocated beneath the distal margin of the annular ligament. One quadrate ligament rupture occurred; the oblique cord and forearm interosseous membrane remained intact.
CONCLUSION: In this standardized cadaveric direct-blow model, anterior radial head dislocation occurred in 11 of 12 limbs, beneath the distal margin of an intact annular ligament. These findings demonstrate that annular ligament rupture is not required for radial head dislocation in the described experimental setting. This mechanism provides a possible anatomic explanation for difficult reduction in selected cases.

title: Low Artificial Intelligence-Estimated Bone Mineral Density From Chest Radiographs Is Associated With Delayed Pain Recovery and Lower Quality of Life After Medial Unicompartmental Knee Arthroplasty.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Whether bone quality influences recovery after medial unicompartmental knee arthroplasty (UKA) remains uncertain, partly because bone mineral density (BMD) is not routinely evaluated using dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry before UKA. This study investigated whether artificial intelligence (AI)-estimated proximal femur BMD derived from preoperative chest radiographs was associated with longitudinal patient-reported outcomes after cemented medial UKA.
METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed 342 consecutive cemented medial UKAs performed from 2012 to 2023. After exclusions, 336 procedures were categorized according to AI-estimated proximal femur young adult mean (YAM), with low estimated BMD defined as YAM less than 80%. Propensity-score matching based on age, sex, body mass index, and diagnosis identified 58 low-BMD procedures and 58 matched controls. Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (KOOS) subscales were evaluated preoperatively and up to three years postoperatively. Linear mixed-effects models assessed group-by-time interactions.
RESULTS: After matching, baseline characteristics were comparable between groups. Both groups demonstrated postoperative improvement across all KOOS subscales. Significant group-by-time interactions were observed for KOOS pain (P < 0.001) and quality of life (QOL) (P = 0.010), whereas no significant interactions were identified for symptoms, activities of daily living, or sport/recreation. The low BMD group had lower pain scores at three months, six months, and one year, as well as lower QOL scores at one, two, and three years. The one-year postoperative range of motion, alignment, component positioning, and radiographic migration or subsidence did not significantly differ between groups.
CONCLUSIONS: Low AI-estimated proximal femur BMD from routine chest radiographs was associated with delayed early pain recovery and statistically lower knee-related QOL from one to three years after cemented medial UKA. Opportunistic AI-based BMD screening may identify candidates for preoperative bone health evaluation and counseling.

title: Culturally Embedded Participation Restrictions in Indian Adults With Knee Osteoarthritis: An ICF-Based Qualitative Study.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To identify culturally relevant functioning issues experienced by Indian adults with knee osteoarthritis (KOA) using the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF) framework.
METHODS: A qualitative descriptive study using semi-structured focus group interviews was conducted with 38 ambulatory adults (35-85 years) diagnosed with knee osteoarthritis (KOA). Participants were recruited from physiotherapy outpatient departments and community settings using maximum variation sampling. Interviews were conducted in Gujarati, audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, translated into English and analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. Meaningful concepts were systematically linked to ICF categories using established linking rules. Dual independent coding and consensus discussions ensured the analytic rigour.
RESULTS: This study included 38 participants with KOA. Fifty-five meaningful second-level categories were identified. The most represented components were activities and participation (41.2%) and body functions (29.4%). Frequently mapped first-level categories included mobility (n = 22), neuromusculoskeletal and movement-related functions (n = 9), d6 domestic life (n = 10), community, social and civic life (n = 7) and products and technology (n = 9). Sixteen additional categories not represented in the existing ICF Core Set for OA emerged, particularly relating to culturally embedded activities such as floor sitting, squatting for toileting and religious participation. Environmental barriers, including inaccessible infrastructure and limited rehabilitation services, influenced disability experience.
CONCLUSION: Functioning among Indian adults with KOA is influenced by culturally embedded participation demands and contextual barriers that are insufficiently captured in the existing ICF Core Set for osteoarthritis (OA). These findings provide preliminary empirical support for contextual validation of the ICF Core Set for OA and inform potential culturally responsive adaptation for KOA.

title: Anatomic feasibility of using Shark Screw tendon for humeral ligament re-construction in medial and posterolateral elbow instability.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Medial and posterolateral rotational instability of the elbow, often resulting from collateral ligament insufficiency, can lead to pain and functional impairment. Surgical re-construction is indicated when conservative treatment fails, yet complications such as graft failure and donor-site morbidity persist. This study investigates the anatomic and biomechanical feasibility of the Shark Screw tendon as a representative human allogeneic bone screw for humeral ligament fixation in cases of elbow instability.
METHODS: Eight fresh-frozen cadaveric specimens were used to evaluate the feasibility of the use of a Shark Screw tendon for humeral fixation on both medial and lateral sides. Cyclic loading and failure testing were performed to assess time-zero fixation characteristics and failure load.
RESULTS: A total of sixteen testing scenarios were conducted on the specimens. Implantation was technically feasible without anatomic limitations related to implant size or positioning. Six graft failures occurred (38%), all attributable to poor tissue quality. Tendon slippage was observed in 9 of 16 cases (56%) under progressively increasing axial load, while the Shark Screw tendon remained seated. The mean failure load was 101 N (±50) for medial insertions, 118 N (±77) for lateral insertions, and 110 N (±64) overall. After 100 cycles, tendon displacement averaged 1.1 mm (±0.4) during extension-flexion on the medial side, 1.0 mm (±1.0) on the lateral side, and 1.0 mm (±0.7) overall. During supination-pronation, displacement was 0.8 mm (±0.7) medially, 1.0 mm (±0.8) laterally, and 0.9 mm (±0.7) overall. No anchor pullout was observed, although one anchor tip fractured during insertion.
CONCLUSION: The Shark Screw tendon appears to be a feasible biologically integrative alternative for humeral fixation in medial and posterolateral elbow ligament re-construction, demonstrating preliminary time-zero fixation characteristics in a cadaveric model. Further biomechanical and clinical studies are needed to confirm long-term outcomes.

title: Stem cell senescence as a regenerative bottleneck in age-related skeletal degeneration: Mechanistic crosstalk and translational strategies.
abstract: Skeletal degeneration is a major cause of pain, disability, fragility fracture, and loss of independence in aging populations. Although osteoporosis, osteoarthritis, and intervertebral disc degeneration are usually managed as anatomically separate disorders, they share a common regenerative failure: endogenous stem and progenitor cells lose renewal capacity, acquire inflammatory secretory programs, and become less able to rebuild damaged matrix. This narrative review synthesizes evidence on senescence in bone marrow mesenchymal stem/stromal cells, skeletal stem cells, hematopoietic stem cells, cartilage progenitor cells, synovial mesenchymal stromal cells, and disc-derived progenitor populations. Priority is given to primary mechanistic, omics, translational, and early clinical studies that connect senescence markers with functional impairment or intervention response. We discuss telomere-associated DNA damage, mitochondrial and oxidative stress, nutrient- and mechanosensing pathways, epigenetic remodeling, dysregulated autophagy and mitophagy, and the senescence-associated secretory phenotype as interlocking mechanisms that reshape skeletal niches. Disease-specific sections then examine how senescent progenitor compartments drive osteoporosis, osteoarthritis, and intervertebral disc degeneration through impaired osteogenesis or chondrogenesis, matrix catabolism, inflammatory vesicle signaling, and maladaptive mechanical feedback. Finally, we compare senolytics, senomorphics, metabolic and mitochondrial regulators, cell rejuvenation, extracellular vesicle engineering, biomaterials, and gene-based delivery platforms from a regenerative medicine perspective. Stem/progenitor cell senescence should be treated not simply as a biomarker of aging, but as a compartment-specific therapeutic bottleneck. Translation will require rigorous cell identity, multi-parameter senescence assays, disease-stage stratification, and therapies that restore regenerative competence without suppressing physiological repair.

title: Post-Exercise Thermal Interventions and Nocturnal Sleep in Athletes: A Narrative Review of the Potential Underlying Physiological Mechanisms.
abstract: Sleep is essential for optimal performance and recovery in athletes. Post-exercise cold exposure, including cold water immersion and cryotherapy, is typically used to enhance recovery, but its effects on sleep remain unclear. Emerging evidence also suggests that post-exercise heat exposure, including sauna and hot water immersion before sleep may improve both objective and subjective sleep outcomes. However, the effectiveness of post-exercise thermal interventions for improving nocturnal sleep in athletes specifically has not yet been comprehensively evaluated. This narrative review synthesizes the current evidence and discusses the potential physiological mechanisms by which post-exercise thermal interventions may influence nocturnal sleep in athletes. Despite methodological heterogeneity, existing research indicates that post-exercise thermal interventions may influence the subsequent nocturnal sleep of athletes through multiple and varying interacting mechanisms. For example, cold exposure close to bedtime (< 2 h) may disrupt sleep by reducing the distal-to-proximal skin temperature gradient (DPG), thereby increasing sleep onset latency and shortening sleep duration. In contrast, when applied more than 2 h before bedtime, cold exposure may improve sleep by augmenting parasympathetic tone and/or reducing muscle soreness and associated nocturnal movement. Although it remains unclear whether post-exercise heat exposure improves sleep via autonomic modulation or reduced muscle soreness, existing evidence indicates that sleep may be facilitated by an increased DPG. Moderating factors such as sex, time of day, environmental temperature, bedding microclimate, acclimatization status, and training load may influence the effects of post-exercise thermal interventions on sleep and should be investigated in future studies.

title: Effect of Pulsed Electromagnetic Stimulation on Delayed Onset Muscle Soreness: Randomized Sham-Controlled Trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The effect of pulsed electromagnetic field (PEMF) therapy on muscle performance and serum creatine kinase (CK) and myoglobin (Mb) values - the biomarkers of muscle damage in experimentally induced delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS) - has yet to be investigated. PEMF therapy is known to be effective to reduce muscle pain, muscle recovery time, fatigue but not to increase muscle force production. The study aimed to compare the effect of PEMF and sham therapy on experimentally induced DOMS in sedentary undergraduate college students.
HYPOTHESIS: PEMF therapy would improve pain, pressure pain threshold (PPT), functional performance, serum CK activity, and Mb concentration compared with the sham intervention.
STUDY DESIGN: Randomized, participant- and assessor-blinded, sham-controlled study.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 2.
METHODS: This study was conducted at Pamukkale University Sarayköy Vocational School. A total of 52 healthy sedentary people received 3 consecutive days of active (Experimental group, n = 26) or sham (Sham group, n = 26) PEMF therapy 24 hours after DOMS induction with a drop-jump protocol. Pain intensity, PPT, functional performance, serum CK activity, and Mb concentration were assessed at baseline, 24 hours and 72 hours after DOMS induction protocol.
RESULTS: The drop-jump protocol induced DOMS successfully in both groups (P < 0.05). All outcome measures were improved in the experimental group (P < 0.05). Mean change scores of PPT (P = 0.53), functional performance (P = 0.10), serum CK (P = 0.38), and Mb concentrations (P = 0.08) were not significantly different between baseline and 72 hours in the sham group. Statistically significant decreases in Mb concentrations were determined in the sham group (P = 0.001).
CONCLUSION: Compared with sham, PEMF therapy improved pain, PPT, functional performance, serum CK activity, and Mb concentration. The duration of PEMF therapy was sufficient to resolve the PPT, functional performance, and serum CK and Mb concentrations associated with DOMS.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This study adds to existing knowledge in showing that, compared with sham, PEMF therapy improved pain, PPT, functional performance, serum CK activity, and Mb concentration.

title: A Practical Pipeline for Patient-Specific Musculoskeletal Modeling: A Comprehensive MRI-Based Framework.
abstract: Patient-specific musculoskeletal (MS) modeling can provide estimates of internal joint loading that canot be measured directly. However, limitations in automated segmentation due to data-scarce environments, morphing difficulty caused by anatomical variability, and functional non-alignment are major bottlenecks that hinder the practical application of modeling and reduce productivity in musculoskeletal research. To comprehensively address these practical issues, this study proposes and validates an integrated, automated modeling framework.. First, we automatically segmented the lower extremity bones of the 4 knee osteoarthritis patients using a multi-atlas-based segmentation algorithm. By integrating the segmented bone with motion capture and force plate data, a modeling pipeline including multi-stage morphing and functional alignment processes was implemented. Using the constructed customized model, the medial and lateral knee contact forces (FMC and FLC) were estimated during a single-leg step-up exercise, and these were compared and evaluated against the results based on manual segmentation. The contact forces estimated through the automated segmentation framework demonstrated high consistency with the manual results. The mean absolute error ranged from 0.04 ± 0.03 to 0.06 ± 0.03 BW for FMC, and from 0.06 ± 0.04 to 0.09 ± 0.07 BW for FLC, and the intraclass correlation coefficient demonstrated a high correlation of over 0.99 across all patients. This study demonstrated that the proposed automated pipeline provides a practical approach to address misalignment caused by anatomical variability, while generating joint load estimates equivalent to the manual approach. By addressing key methodological challenges, this study will bring patient-specific models closer to future clinical application, where they could help assess individual loading across different activities and inform treatment and rehabilitation strategies.

title: A Translational Approach for Treatment of Posterior Cruciate Ligament Injuries: From Foundational Anatomic and Biomechanical Studies to Validated Surgical Outcomes.
abstract: Posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) injuries were historically managed nonsurgically or with primary repairs, owing to limited anatomic knowledge, subjective diagnostic techniques, and nonvalidated reconstructions that frequently failed. We describe a two-decade, bench-to-bedside PCL research pyramid that progressively addressed these deficiencies. Foundational cadaveric work characterized the quantitative anatomy of the PCL, including the anterolateral and posteromedial bundles, yielding reproducible femoral and tibial osseous landmarks for tunnel placement. Robotic biomechanical testing established the codominant contribution of both bundles, optimal graft fixation angles, and the destabilizing influence of posterolateral corner injuries and flat tibial slope. Objective diagnostic methods, such as kneeling PCL stress radiography and posterior tibial translation on MRI, were validated to quantify laxity and detect chronic tears. These insights informed an anatomically grounded double-bundle reconstruction, complemented by multiligament tunnel convergence-avoidance strategies, evidence-based tensioning sequences, and a refined rehabilitation and bracing treatment protocol. Prospective outcome studies confirmed restoration of stability comparable to anterior cruciate ligament reconstructions, demonstrating how integrated translational research transformed treatment of this challenging injury.

title: Enhancing Sleep in NCAA Division I Athletes: A Study of Sleep Extension Feasibility.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Sleep extension has been shown to improve varied aspects of athletic performance in collegiate athletes. Such studies have been conducted in small cohorts in controlled settings utilizing obsolete monitoring technology. The feasibility of sleep extension has not been evaluated in a broader cohort of collegiate athletes with modern monitoring technology.
HYPOTHESIS: Sleep extension may not be feasible in National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA) Division I athletes.
STUDY DESIGN: Crossover study.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 3.
METHODS: Baseline sleep data were collected from NCAA Division I athletes (women's soccer, men's soccer, baseball, and football) during a 2-week period. Subjects were then instructed to extend their total sleep time to 10 hours per night for 2 weeks. All sleep baseline and extension data were collected in the offseason, remote from school examinations. WHOOP bands recorded all sleep metrics. Data were analyzed using paired-samples t tests and Wilcoxon signed rank tests.
RESULTS: A total of 50 subjects (14 female, 36 male) participated. The study compared total sleep time (hours) and sleep consistency (percent) - the stability of sleep-wake schedule over time, between baseline and sleep extension phases. Sample size varied for both metrics, ranging from 46 to 49 participants, respectively. There was a statistically significant increase in sleep consistency during the sleep extension phase (baseline, 60.09 ± 12.6%; extension, 64.42 ± 12.4%; P = 0.02). However, total sleep time showed no significant difference between the 2 phases (baseline, 7.63 ± 0.88 hours; extension, 7.51 ± 0.88 hours; P = 0.27).
CONCLUSION: Extension efforts improved sleep consistency but did not significantly impact total sleep time suggesting that a sleep extension intervention can enhance sleep consistency in NCAA Division I athletes but does not significantly impact total sleep time. Sleep extension may be challenging for collegiate athletes given the time-intensive demands of both academics and sports. While sleep extension may be feasible in professional sports, it does not appear to be so in the college setting.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: While the sleep extension intervention improved sleep consistency, it did not improve total sleep time, questioning the feasibility of sleep extension in collegiate sports.

title: Ask the experts: a practitioner-centred approach to resilience in emergency medical services.
abstract: Background: Resilience in high-stress occupations is commonly framed as a trait, an outcome, or the absence of psychopathology. None of these framings captures what practitioners in emergency medical services actually do, and interventions built on trait-based models have produced weak or inconsistent effects.Objective: This study argues that frontline resilience in emergency medical services is better understood as a domain-specific expert skill, and that work mode - a deliberately entered state, akin to an athlete's game face, in which the demands of the task rather than the emotional force of the scene govern functioning - is its central empirical signature. The aims were to identify factors that intensify traumatic impact, characterise the strategies practitioners use to maintain functioning, and explore systemic and relational barriers that constrain coping.Method: Twenty Queensland Ambulance Service paramedics and dispatchers (tenure 2-38 years) participated in semi-structured interviews, analysed via reflexive thematic analysis.Results: Three intensifiers of traumatic impact (unpredictability, moral weight, personal threat) defined the operational demands against which resilience was enacted. Three coping themes (baseline buffers, work mode, social scaffolding) described the architecture of sustained functioning. Work mode exhibited the defining features of skilled performance: domain specificity, a phased temporal structure (preparation, containment, recovery), and a developmental trajectory from effortful to automatic execution. Two further themes (organisational distrust, the outsider gap) described the systemic and relational conditions that constrain coping.Conclusions: Treating resilience as expertise shifts the field from descriptive stressor-outcome accounts towards assessable, trainable capacities, and exposes the limitations of trait-based self-report measures that cannot distinguish genuine resilience from unsustainable stoicism.

title: An Intensified Training Period Reduces REM Sleep but this Decline Can Be Mitigated by Ketone Ester Supplementation.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: We previously showed that a strenuous training day disrupts sleep efficiency and REM sleep, and that these disturbances can be counteracted by ketone monoester (R)-3-hydroxybutyl-(R)-3-hydroxybutyrate (KE) supplementation. However, the impact of prolonged intensified training on sleep quality, as well as the potential modulating effect of KE are unknown.
METHODS: We performed a double-blind study in which twenty-four trained male athletes completed a 7-week training program with a gradual increase in training load while receiving either 25g of a control drink (CON, n=12) or 25g of KE (n=12) after each training session and 30 minutes before sleep. At the start (PRE), week 3 (MID), and the end (POST) of the training program, we evaluated sleep using polysomnography, and perceived stress/recovery balance using the REST-Q questionnaire. Timing, duration, and relative intensity of exercise on each testing day were identical.
RESULTS: The progressive increase in training load induced a decrease in the perceived stress-recovery state in both groups (PRE: 73±21 vs. POST: 40±37, p<0.001, Hedges' g = 1.097). From PRE to MID, sleep efficiency improved by 3% in both groups (p=0.003, Hedges' g = 0.663) while wakefulness after sleep onset reduced by 2% (p=0.031, Hedges' g = 0.716). However, from PRE to POST, total REM sleep decreased by 2% in CON but increased by 3% in KE (p=0.002, for KE vs. CON, Hedges' g = 0.939). Perceived sleep quality did not differ between groups throughout the intervention.
CONCLUSIONS: Our data indicate that KE supplementation did not enhance the beneficial effect of an initial increase in training load on sleep but prevented the decline in REM sleep upon a further training load increment.

title: The effect of positive emotions on psychophysiological recovery and performance in athletes - investigating the undoing-hypothesis.
abstract: Athletes have to cope with psychosocial and physiological stressors, requiring recovery to ensure subsequent performance. According to the undoing-hypothesis, positive emotions (PE) may enhance psychophysiological recovery. The present two studies investigated the undoing hypothesis and its benefits for athletes' cognitive (Study 1; n = 60) and motor (Study 2; n = 30) performance. After a combined psychosocial-physiological stressor, participants either completed a five-minute PE induction (music; imagination exercise) or were assigned to a resting condition. Emotions, perceived stress-recovery, and physiological parameters (e.g., heart rate, heart rate variability, cortisol) were assessed. In Study 1, inhibition and cognitive flexibility were measured once. In Study 2, hand force and jump height were measured using a pre-posttest design. Due to the lack of psychological stress responses and successful PE induction, no conclusions could be drawn regarding the undoing hypothesis. Nevertheless, the present study provides valuable methodological insights into the challenges of testing the undoing hypothesis in athletes. These insights can inform the design and implementation of future studies and thereby contribute to advancing research on the undoing hypothesis in athletic populations.

title: Bilateral Lower-Body Force Asymmetry and Countermovement Jump Performance of South African Amateur Padel Athletes.
abstract: The countermovement jump (CMJ) is a widely used assessment of lower-limb power and neuromuscular function. The physical demands of padel, including repeated accelerations, decelerations, changes of direction, jumping, and landing, may contribute to inter-limb asymmetries influencing performance and injury risk. This quantitative cross-sectional study investigated lower-limb asymmetries during the CMJ in amateur (non-professional) padel athletes. Thirty participants (mean age: 41.2 ± 14.5 years; 63% male, 37% female) completed bilateral CMJ assessments using VALD (Brisbane, Australia) ForceDecks force plates. Outcome measures included concentric, eccentric, and landing peak force, peak power, rate of force development and jump height. Significant dominant-limb advantages were identified for concentric (p = 0.002), eccentric (p = 0.024), and landing peak force (p = 0.044). Male athletes demonstrated greater jump heights than female athletes (p < 0.001), while female athletes exhibited greater landing-phase force asymmetry (p = 0.004). Amateur padel athletes display significant inter-limb asymmetries in force production across the concentric, eccentric, and landing phases of the CMJ, with greater force generation in the dominant limb. Furthermore, the greater landing asymmetry observed in female athletes may reflect reduced inter-limb load distribution during landing tasks. These results highlight the value of CMJ assessment in identifying neuromuscular asymmetries that may influence performance and increase injury risk in padel athletes.

title: Concussion symptom clusters and changes in symptom reporting and severity following multiple concussions in male professional rugby league players.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Symptom reporting remains an important part of the diagnosis and management of concussion. Understanding the patterns of symptoms and symptom clusters in athletes with multiple concussions may be clinically valuable. The purpose of this study was to characterise acute symptom reporting in players with multiple concussions.
METHODS: National Rugby League (NRL) players who have sustained multiple concussions between the 2017 and 2022 seasons were included in the study. Data included the symptoms reported on the Sport Concussion Assessment Tool - 5th Edition (SCAT5) during the Head Injury Assessment by players who were subsequently diagnosed with concussion. K-means clustering with k = 6 centres was performed on symptom severity data. Each concussion episode was assigned to one symptom cluster based on the athlete's symptom presentation. Transitions between symptom clusters from initial to subsequent concussions were visualised using a Sankey plot.
RESULTS: There were 120 players who sustained more than one concussion, including 75 players with two, 23 with three, 15 with four, and 7 players with five or more medically diagnosed concussions. The average duration between concussions was 441 days (SD: 332; Md: 370; range: 11-1435 days). There were 6 different symptom clusters identified. Players were commonly found to transition between clusters for subsequent concussions, most commonly the 'Asymptomatic' cluster. There was no relationship found for days between concussions and symptom count or severity. Symptom severity, but not symptom count, was associated with days until medical clearance.
CONCLUSION: Acute symptom reporting varies with subsequent concussions, making it difficult to predict post-concussion symptoms in individual players. Acute symptom severity was associated with time to medical clearance, whereas the number of concussions in the preceding two years was not.

title: Exercise Is Associated with Skeletal Muscle Autophagy-Lysosome-Related Markers and Nrf2/ARF1 Signaling in HFD Mice.
abstract: Purpose: This study aimed to investigate the protective effects and potential mechanisms of exercise against long-term high-fat diet (HFD)-induced skeletal muscle dysfunction, with a focus on ADP-ribosylation factor 1 (ARF1)-related autophagy-lysosome markers and nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2) signaling. Methods: Forty male C57BL/6 mice were randomly divided into a normal diet group (DC) and an HFD group, and the latter was further subdivided into a model group (MG), exercise group (EG), Nrf2 inhibitor group (NG), and exercise combined with Nrf2 inhibitor group (ENG) after 12 weeks of HFD feeding. EG received 6 weeks of moderate-intensity treadmill exercise, NG was treated with Nrf2 inhibitor for 6 weeks, and ENG received both the 6-week treadmill exercise and inhibitor injections simultaneously. Serum lipid, blood glucose and insulin resistance indices were detected; skeletal muscle morphology was observed by H&E staining; mRNA and protein expression of ARF1, ULK1, ATP6V0A1 and other factors were determined by RT-qPCR, Western blotting and immunohistochemistry; the oxidative stress index was measured by an ELISA; and the colocalization of ARF1/ATP6V0A1 with the lysosomal marker Lamp1 was analyzed by immunofluorescence. Results: Long-term HFD significantly increased mouse body weight, serum TC, TG, LDL-C, FBG levels and the HOMA-IR index, induced morphological alterations in skeletal muscle (loose myofiber arrangement, abundant intracellular vacuoles), inhibited the mRNA expression of ARF1, ULK1 and ATP6V0A1, and elevated malondialdehyde (MDA) content (p < 0.05 or p < 0.01). Six weeks of moderate-intensity treadmill exercise effectively improved HFD-induced metabolic disorders and skeletal muscle morphological damage, upregulated the expression of ARF1, ULK1 and ATP6V0A1, and reduced oxidative stress (p < 0.05 or p < 0.01). Notably, luteolin-mediated inhibition of Nrf2 signaling may partially reverse exercise-induced alterations in ARF1-related autophagy-lysosome markers and skeletal muscle morphology. Conclusions: Long-term HFD may induce morphological alterations in skeletal muscle, accompanied by changes in ARF1-associated autophagy-lysosome markers and elevated oxidative stress. Conversely, moderate-intensity exercise may ameliorate HFD-related changes in skeletal muscle morphology, potentially via Nrf2 signaling, providing a potential molecular target and theoretical basis for the exercise intervention strategies against HFD-induced metabolic-related skeletal muscle dysfunction.

title: Sleep Characteristics of Elite Female Soccer Players Competing in the National Women's Soccer League Across a Competitive Season.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Sleep supports recovery and readiness in professional sport, yet season-long objective data in women's professional soccer are limited. This study aimed to provide a longitudinal, objective description of sleep across a competitive season and to compare sleep characteristics between preseason and in-season phases.
METHODS: Twenty-seven professional athletes were monitored from January to November 2024 using a finger-worn wearable. Nightly total sleep time (TST), sleep efficiency, sleep onset latency (SOL), and sleep stage durations were extracted. Preseason versus in-season differences were examined using linear mixed-effects models and reported as estimated marginal mean differences with 95% CIs.
RESULTS: During the in-season, TST averaged 7.8 (1.2) hours (median: 7.9 h), sleep efficiency 89.1% (5.4%), and SOL 15.6 (12.6) minutes. Mean sleep stage durations were 262.8 (52.8) minutes (light), 96.6 (31.8) minutes (deep), and 106.8 (34.2) minutes (Rapid Eye Movement). Notable night-to-night variability was observed, particularly for TST (within-player coefficients of variation: 10%-18%) and SOL (50%-114%). Compared with preseason, in-season sleep was characterized by lower REM sleep (-4.8 min, 95% CI -6.9 to -2.8; P < .001), reduced sleep efficiency (-0.37%, 95% CI -0.71 to -0.02; P = .036), and shorter SOL (-1.1 min, 95% CI -2.0 to -0.2; P = .020). TST did not differ between phases (P = .287), and deep and light sleep remained unchanged. Effect sizes were small (Cohen d ≤ 0.15).
CONCLUSIONS: Group averages of sleep parameters might mask individual and seasonal changes in sleep, highlighting the need for longitudinal, athlete-specific monitoring to guide proactive sleep monitoring strategies.

title: Cardiac autonomic and hemodynamic responses to two-stage cycling and post-exercise recovery with partial blood flow restriction in young males.
abstract:
PURPOSE: This study compared acute cardiovascular and cardiac autonomic responses during graded (two-stage) aerobic cycling and subsequent recovery performed with and without partial blood flow restriction (BFR).
METHODS: Fifteen young males completed two sessions in a crossover design (control vs. bilateral thigh BFR). Each session included rest, 5 min of cycling at 40% maximal power output (Pmax), 5 min at 60% Pmax, and 10 min of recovery; BFR was released immediately at exercise cessation. ECG and arterial blood pressure were recorded. RR interval, mean arterial blood pressure (MBP), HRV (lnRMSSD, lnSDNN, HF, LF, LF/HF), and composite indices of cardiac sympathetic and parasympathetic activity (SNS, PNS) were derived from 3-min segments at rest, exercise, and recovery. Heart rate recovery at 30, 60, and 120 s after exercise cessation (HRR30, HRR60, HRR120) was calculated. Two-way repeated-measures ANOVA tested condition, time, and interaction.
RESULTS: Time × condition interactions were observed for RR interval (p=0.015) and MBP (p=0.003), indicating altered hemodynamic kinetics under BFR, primarily during recovery. HRV indices showed no time × condition interactions; however, BFR produced lower lnRMSSD, lnSDNN, HF, and PNS and higher SNS than control (all p<0.05), whereas LF and LF/HF were unchanged. HRR30 (p=0.040), HRR60 (p<0.001), and HRR120 (p=0.010) were attenuated under BFR.
CONCLUSIONS: BFR modifies cardiovascular regulation during two-stage cycling and recovery and induces sustained autonomic shifts toward reduced parasympathetic and increased sympathetic modulation, largely independent of exercise intensity. Altered recovery kinetics following cuff release highlight the importance of careful monitoring during the recovery phase when applying BFR.

title: Post-COVID-19 Penalty Trends Following an Injury-Prevention Rule Change in Rhode Island High School Boys' Hockey.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Penalty infraction minute (PIM)-based rule modifications have been implemented in youth and high school ice hockey to reduce injury risk. A prior Rhode Island Interscholastic League (RIIL) study demonstrated a reduction in game-related injuries following implementation of a statewide 2015-2016 50/70 PIM rule. The durability of these behavioral trends post-COVID-19 has not been evaluated.
PURPOSE: This descriptive epidemiologic study evaluates post-pandemic trends in penalty infraction minutes and disqualifying penalties in RIIL boys' varsity ice hockey.
METHODS: Publicly available RIIL varsity boys' ice hockey data were reviewed for four consecutive seasons (2021-2022 through 2024-2025). Extracted variables included total rostered players, counts of players exceeding PIM thresholds (≥25, ≥50, ≥70), mean team PIM per game, goals scored, number of participating teams, and total disqualifying penalties per season. Data were summarized descriptively by season.
RESULTS: Across four seasons, rostered players ranged from 479 to 540, with 21 to 25 teams competing annually. Mean team PIM per game remained stable, ranging from 8.13 to 8.83. No players accumulated ≥50 or ≥70 PIM in any season. Players accumulating ≥25 PIM ranged from 17 to 24 per season. Disqualifying penalties occurred each season (range, 5-11 per year) without a consistent directional trend. Goals scored remained proportional to participating teams.
CONCLUSIONS: In post-pandemic seasons, PIM distributions and disqualifying penalties remained stable, with no recurrence of high-PIM accumulations requiring suspension. These findings suggest sustained behavioral patterns following rule modifications, but cannot be interpreted as evidence of injury reduction without injury surveillance data. Continued monitoring incorporating injury outcomes is warranted.

title: TAICHIKNEE trial: protocol for an embedded pragmatic, individually randomised group-treatment trial of remotely delivered Tai Chi for knee osteoarthritis across US healthcare systems.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Symptomatic knee osteoarthritis (OA) is a leading cause of chronic pain and disability and is associated with substantial healthcare utilisation and costs. In-person Tai Chi, a multidimensional mind-body exercise, is recommended as a non-pharmacological therapy for knee OA; however, delivery through in-person classes may limit scalability across US healthcare systems. Remote delivery may reduce logistical barriers and facilitate integration into routine care, but evidence regarding its effectiveness and implementation in real-world healthcare settings remains limited. We describe the protocol for TAICHIKNEE, an embedded pragmatic trial evaluating remotely delivered group Tai Chi plus routine care vs routine care alone for adults with symptomatic knee OA.
METHODS AND ANALYSIS: TAICHIKNEE is a 12-month, fully decentralised, embedded pragmatic, individually randomised group-treatment trial with an effectiveness-implementation hybrid type 1 design conducted across five US healthcare systems. The trial will randomise 480 adults aged ≥50 years with symptomatic, clinician-diagnosed knee OA in a 1:1 ratio within six sequential cohorts, stratified by healthcare system and sex. Participants assigned to Tai Chi will receive 24 live, instructor-led 60-minute videoconference sessions over 12 weeks in addition to routine care; control participants will continue routine care. The cohort randomisation date defines time zero for both groups. The primary outcome is Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC) pain at 3 months, analysed using a partially nested mixed-effects model that accounts for clustering within Tai Chi classes and adjusts for baseline WOMAC pain and prespecified covariates. Key secondary outcomes are Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System Pain Interference and SF-12 health-related quality of life scores at 3 months, and knee joint injections over 12 months. Safety will be assessed throughout the 12-month follow-up. The implementation evaluation will concurrently assess intervention fidelity, stakeholder perspectives and participant and instructor experiences using Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research-informed stakeholder interviews, fidelity assessments and surveys to identify factors influencing implementation and inform future sustainment and spread across healthcare systems.
ETHICS AND DISSEMINATION: Ethical approval was obtained from the Tufts University Health Sciences Institutional Review Board (IRB) (STUDY00003780), serving as the single IRB of record for all participating sites. Results will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publications, conferences and stakeholder engagement activities across healthcare systems. De-identified participant-level data and study materials will be shared in accordance with applicable data-sharing policies, participant consent, IRB requirements and the approved data-sharing plan.

title: Breaking limits: rapid sea-to-summit ascent of Mount Everest (8,848 m) in 3 days 23 hours following normobaric-hypoxic pre-acclimatization and staged supplemental oxygen in a non-elite athlete.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Traditional ascent of Mount Everest (8,848 m) typically requires 40-50 days of on-mountain acclimatization. Normobaric hypoxia (NH) pre-acclimatization is a practical home-based alternative; however, no peer-reviewed case report has described a sea-to-summit Everest ascent completed in under four days by a non-elite individual without prior on-mountain acclimatization rotations.
METHODS: A 40-year-old male recreational mountaineer (baseline VO2max 40.8 ml·kg-1·min-1; BMI 30.1 kg·m-2) completed an 18-week structured NH pre-acclimatization program comprising 48 nights of hypoxic sleep (~377 h at simulated altitudes of 1,850-5,486 m; FiO2 16.7-10.5%) and 16 hypoxic exercise sessions (34 h at 3,085-6,000 m; FiO2 14.3-9.8%). Hypoxic dose was calculated as Σ[(95/SpO2 - 1) × h × 100]. During the climb, peripheral oxygen saturation (SpO2) and heart rate (HR) were recorded at each camp, and acute mountain sickness (AMS) was assessed using the 2018 Lake Louise Score (LLS). Supplemental oxygen (O2) was initiated at 0.5 L·min-1 at the start of the ascent from Everest Base Camp (EBC, 5,360 m) and titrated to SpO2 and symptoms up to 3.0 L·min-1 during the summit push.
RESULTS: The program yielded a combined hypoxic exposure of 411 h and a cumulative hypoxic dose of 4,779%·h (sleep 4,353%·h; exercise 426%·h). VO2max increased from 40.8 to 51.0 ml·kg-1·min-1, and body mass decreased from 118.1 to 101.5 kg. The subject departed New York at 00:30 local time (EDT; 10:15 Nepal Standard Time, NST) on 15 May 2025 and reached the summit at 09:22 NST on 19 May 2025, a total sea-to-summit time of 3 days, 23 hours and 7 minutes; the ascent from EBC to the summit took 60 hours and 22 minutes. SpO2 was 75% at Camp 3 (7,100 m; HR 95 bpm) and 70% on arrival at Camp 4 (7,950 m; HR 105 bpm) and at the summit (HR 105 bpm). On descent, SpO2 recovered to 80% at Camp 4 and 85% at Camp 2 (6,750 m; HR 110 bpm), and was 85% on room air on return to EBC (HR 62 bpm). No AMS was diagnosed during the ascent (LLS 0-1 at all ascending checkpoints); mild AMS criteria were met on descent (LLS = 3), resolving by return to EBC. No high-altitude cerebral or pulmonary edema occurred.
DISCUSSION: To our knowledge, this case documents the fastest recorded sea-to-summit ascent of Mount Everest by a non-professional athlete. The combination of a structured 18-week NH pre-acclimatization program, objective physiological monitoring, and staged supplemental oxygen, together with the absence of severe altitude-related complications, suggests that rapid ascent without traditional on-mountain acclimatization may be feasible in a well-prepared, closely supervised non-elite individual. Controlled prospective studies are required to quantify the relative contributions of hematological, ventilatory, and mitochondrial adaptations induced by high-dose NH exposure.

title: Eating Behavior, Body Appreciation, and Sleep Quality in Italian Blind Baseball Athletes: A Cross-Sectional Exploratory Survey.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Visual impairment is associated with poor sleep quality, psychological distress, and unhealthy lifestyle behaviors. Adapted sports, such as blind baseball (BXC), may help promote healthy lifestyles and overall well-being. However, evidence regarding eating behavior, sleep quality, body appreciation, and lifestyle habits among regular BXC players remains scarce. This cross-sectional study provides an exploratory multidimensional characterization of these domains in competitive Italian BXC athletes according to sport participation and visual impairment characteristics, comparing findings descriptively with normative data from the Italian general population. Methods: Fifty-three competitive Italian BXC players (mean age 39.3 ± 13.1 years; representing a response rate of 49.1% of the national league) completed an anonymous online survey assessing eating behavior (Adult Eating Behavior Questionnaire, AEBQ), body appreciation (Body Appreciation Scale-2, BAS-2), sleep quality (Brief Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index, B-PSQI), and lifestyle habits. Group differences were assessed using chi-square tests for categorical variables and Mann-Whitney U tests for continuous variables, reporting medians, interquartile ranges, effect sizes (rank-biserial r), and 95% confidence intervals. Results: BXC athletes demonstrated BMI, sleep quality, eating behavior, and body appreciation profiles comparable to those of the Italian general population. BAS-2 scores were high (3.7-3.8), while B-PSQI scores (4.0-5.6) and the proportion of poor sleepers (~40%) remained within normative ranges despite visual impairment. Eating behavior showed no significant dysregulation. However, in exploratory subgroup analyses, multisport athletes displayed lower Satiety Responsiveness than BXC-only athletes (2.30 ± 0.79 vs. 2.78 ± 0.71; p = 0.02), poorer sleep quality (B-PSQI: 6.05 ± 3.12 vs. 4.70 ± 3.73; p = 0.05), and a higher prevalence of poor sleep (55.0% vs. 30.3%). Athletes with acquired visual impairment showed higher Emotional Overeating and Emotional Undereating scores than those with congenital impairment, although these differences did not reach statistical significance. Conclusions: BXC athletes displayed an overall favorable lifestyle profile. Though the cross-sectional design prevents causal inferences, these exploratory findings indicate that participation in BXC is compatible with healthy lifestyle habits and positive body appreciation, hence supporting adapted team sports as an inclusive framework for multidimensional health promotion. Future studies using objective physiological assessments and longitudinal designs are needed to clarify dose-response relationships and long-term health outcomes.

title: Talking about menstruation in professional women's sport: gendered communication between athletes, coaches and team-mates.
abstract: Communication about menstruation remains uneven within sporting environments despite growing recognition of the importance of menstrual health for athletes. This article investigates how female athletes communicate about menstruation and how gendered hierarchies shape these interactions. The analysis is based on responses to an online questionnaire completed by Polish professional athletes (N = 253). The findings indicate that menstruation is seldom discussed between athletes and coaches, with participants identifying social and institutional barriers, including menstrual taboo and the predominance of male coaches. In contrast, athletes reported discussing menstruation more openly with female team-mates, where such conversations often facilitated mutual support and the sharing of experiential knowledge about menstrual health. These interactions suggest that women's teams can function as 'counterspaces' where menstrual experiences can be acknowledged and normalised in ways largely absent from coach-athlete relationships. Findings highlight the importance of creating environments in which menstrual health can be openly discussed, as limited communication about menstruation may restrict athletes' access to information, support, and health-related guidance. By examining menstruation as a topic of health-related communication, the study contributes to scholarship on gender, embodiment and menstrual health, highlighting how institutional hierarchies shape the visibility and discussion of bodily processes across different social contexts.

title: Progression of peak athletic performance age in the past four decades.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Older athletes are redefining the prime by extending their athletic longevity. A trend that women's peak performance age tends to increase, while men's remains largely unchanged, has been reported some time ago. The present study builds on this early work by examining more recent data to determine whether such gender differences persisted across contemporary periods and in different sporting events.
METHODS: Ages of Olympic medalists from 1984 to 2024 were analyzed as indicators of peak performance age (N.=2016).
RESULTS: In men, peak performance ages ranged 26±2 to 28±2 years in endurance, 26±2 to 27±2 years in power, 23±1 to 24±2 years in sprint, and 26±2 to 27±2 years in skill. In women, the ranges were from 27±2 to 29±2 years for endurance, 26±2 to 28±2 years for power, 23±2 to 24±2 years for sprint, and 23±3 to 26±3 years for skill. There were no gender differences in peak performance age among endurance, power, and sprint events in any era. However, in skill sports, male athletes demonstrated a higher peak performance age in 1984-1996 (P<0.05), a difference that has since disappeared. The age variabilities show an upward trend over time in both men and women.
CONCLUSIONS: We concluded that in recent years, both male and female athletes have achieved peak performance at comparable ages across all sport types.

title: High Ubiquitin-like Protein 3 Expression Is Associated With Prolonged Recurrence-free Survival in Non-muscle-invasive Bladder Cancer.
abstract:
BACKGROUND/AIM: Current clinicopathological factors inadequately capture the biological heterogeneity of non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC). This study investigated the prognostic significance of ubiquitin-like protein 3 (UBL3), a molecule involved in extracellular vesicle sorting and immune regulation, in NMIBC.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: Following an exploratory analysis of public RNA-sequencing databases, we evaluated tissue samples from patients who underwent transurethral resection for primary NMIBC. A discovery cohort (n=37) was assessed for UBL3 mRNA via qRT-PCR and protein expression via immunohistochemistry (IHC) quantified using digital H-scores (QuPath). A separate internal validation cohort (n=192) was subsequently evaluated by IHC. The primary endpoint was recurrence-free survival (RFS).
RESULTS: The database analysis indicated that high UBL3 expression was associated with longer RFS in early-stage bladder cancer. In the discovery cohort, higher UBL3 mRNA levels were associated with prolonged RFS [hazard ratio (HR)=0.33, p=0.004]. mRNA levels also were associated with digital H-scores (ρ=0.39, p=0.018). In the separate internal validation cohort, elevated UBL3 protein expression was associated with a reduced risk of recurrence. A multivariable Cox regression confirmed that a higher UBL3 H-score (HR=0.95 per 10-point increase, p=0.023), alongside a negative preoperative urine cytology and immediate intravesical chemotherapy, remained independently associated with RFS.
CONCLUSION: Elevated UBL3 expression was associated with prolonged RFS in patients with NMIBC following transurethral resection of bladder tumor. While UBL3 has potential as a prognostic biomarker, establishing its definitive clinical utility will require mechanistic investigations and validation across independent, multicenter cohorts.

title: Test-Retest Reliability of Soft Tissue Vibration Variables Across an Outdoor 5-km Run.
abstract: The purpose of this study was to determine the test-retest reliability of soft tissue vibration (STV) measurements taken superficial to the medial gastrocnemius during a 5-km outdoor run. Twenty-eight trained athlete participants (female: n = 14 and male: n = 14) wore a triaxial inertial measurement unit mounted on the skin superficial to their medial gastrocnemius (500 Hz) and performed two 5-km outdoor runs on different days at a controlled, individualized pace. STV outcome measures-peak acceleration, damping coefficient, settling time, peak and median frequency, and power-were analyzed using a continuous wavelet transform from averaged running strides within the entire run and among three 1500-m segments from each testing session. Intraclass correlation coefficients reinforced good to excellent between-day reliability measures (.75-.92) for all STV outcome measures except peak frequency (.50) and moderate to excellent reliability when comparing days across the 3 segments of the run (.70-.94), except for peak frequency (.44-.57). No significant day × time interactions were observed (P = .06-.63). Overall, STV outcome measures assessed with an inertial measurement unit during outdoor running demonstrated good reliability, supporting methodologies to quantify STV in real-world settings with potential applications in running performance and injury prevention research.

title: Investigational Peptides in Orthopaedic Practice: Evidence, Safety, and Patient Counseling for BPC-157, Thymosin Beta-4, and TB-500.
abstract: Peptide-based products, particularly Body Protection Compound-157 (BPC-157), and thymosin beta-4 (TB-4), and products marketed as TB-500, are increasingly promoted for musculoskeletal recovery despite limited clinical validation. This narrative review evaluated their molecular rationale, direct musculoskeletal evidence, human safety and efficacy data, product quality concerns, regulatory status, antidoping implications, and relevance to orthopaedic counseling. PubMed/MEDLINE, EMBASE, and Scopus were searched from inception through June 2026, with additional review of primary regulatory and antidoping sources. BPC-157 has the largest bod of direct musculoskeletal preclinical evidence, including predominantly small-animal studies involving tendon, ligament, muscle, inflammatory joint disease, and bone. However, human musculoskeletal evidence is limited to one small retrospective uncontrolled case series without validated outcome measures. Validated dosing, pharmacokinetic, and long-term safety data are lacking. TB-4 has broader experimental and human experience in ophthalmic, dermatologic, and cardiovascular applications, but direct musculoskeletal evidence remains limited to in vitro and rodent studies. These nonorthopaedic findings cannot establish musculoskeletal efficacy or safety. TB-500 is a distinct seven amino-acid fragment of TB-4 that is frequently conflated with full-length TB-4 despite the absence of validated biologic or clinical equivalence. Commercial products marketed also raise concerns regarding identity, purity, concentration, sterility, and manufacturing consistency. None of these agents has an FDA-approved musculoskeletal indication, validated orthopaedic treatment protocol, or controlled human orthopaedic efficacy evidence. Orthopaedic clinicians should specifically ask about peptide use, distinguish preclinical plausibility from clinical validation, address product quality and safety uncertainties, and counsel athletes regarding antidoping restrictions. Routine clinical use cannot be currently recommended.

title: Relationship Between Objective Measures of Sleep and Nocturnal Cardiovascular Physiology and Swimming Performance in Collegiate Female Athletes: A Bayesian Analysis.
abstract: Vatne, EA, Cencer, D, Vatne, M, Pulvermacher, K, Saenz, C, Kraemer, WJ, Robinson, B, Jones, P, Quebedeaux, N, Sprague, R, Dial, M, Carpenter, T, and Hagen, J. Relationship between objective measures of sleep and nocturnal cardiovascular physiology and swimming performance in collegiate female athletes: A Bayesian analysis. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-There is substantial evidence that sleep influences athletic performance; however, relationships with real-world competition outcomes remain unclear. Therefore, the purpose of this study was to explore the associations between objectively measured sleep, nocturnal cardiovascular physiology on the night before competition, and swim performance in female collegiate athletes. Female swimmers (n = 11) who wore a sleep monitoring device the night before competition, competed in the 200-yard freestyle (short course yard), and had ≥21 of 28 prior nights of valid data were included. Sleep metrics included total sleep time (TST), time in bed (TiB), and sleep efficiency (SE), whereas nocturnal cardiovascular metrics included heart rate variability (HRV) and resting heart rate (RHR) standardized as individualized z-scores. Race times were obtained from a publicly available database. Bayesian linear mixed-effects models estimated posterior probabilities of performance improvement. Results indicated a high probability that greater TST and TiB were associated with faster race times, with substantial support for improvements of at least 1 second per additional hour of sleep. In contrast, SE, HRV, and RHR showed low posterior evidence of meaningful associations with performance. These findings extend prior sleep and performance literature that has been confined to proxy assessments of athletic performance in controlled settings to real-world competition that should inform athlete education, emphasizing the importance of sufficient sleep opportunity and duration before competition.

title: Gender Differences in Sports Injuries of the Foot and Ankle.
abstract: This article examines sex-based differences in foot and ankle injuries among female athletes, emphasizing the role of anatomic, hormonal, biomechanical, and sociocultural factors. Female athletes are disproportionately affected by ankle sprains, chronic instability, and bone stress injuries. Conditions such as relative energy deficiency in sport and the female athlete triad contribute to injury risk and long-term health consequences but remain under-recognized. This article highlights disparities in research, treatment, and outcomes, calling for improved screening, sex-specific prevention strategies, and greater inclusion of female subjects in sports medicine research to inform evidence-based care and optimize outcomes for female athletes.

title: Open and closed-chain shoulder joint position sense: inter-day reliability and normative profiles in male contact sport athletes.
abstract: The purpose was to determine inter-day reliability and normative values for open and closed-chain shoulder joint position sense (JPS). Male contact and collision sport athletes (18-40 years) participated in two study phases. Sixteen athletes completed open- and closed-chain JPS tests on two occasions (2-9 days apart) to determine inter-day reliability. Twenty-eight athletes completed the same protocol on one occasion to establish normative profiles. Open-chain JPS was assessed in a standing position using shoulder flexion to pre-defined angles with a laser pointer (55°, 90° and 125° of humerothoracic flexion; no haptic target); closed-chain JPS was assessed in a push-up position by reproducing target positions (chest lowered onto a hurdle at 16.5 cm [low] or 30.5 cm [high]; an initial haptic target). Three-dimensional kinematics quantified repositioning errors. Intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC) and standard error of measurement (SEM) were calculated for reliability. Pearson correlations were calculated between open and closed-chain errors. Open-chain tests demonstrated moderate reliability across both arms (ICCs = 0.71-0.74), with better reliability on the dominant limb (ICCs = 0.68-0.90) compared to the non-dominant (ICCs = 0.43-0.55). SEM values ranged from 0.70 to 2.03°. Closed-chain tests showed poor reliability at the high target (ICC = 0.49) but good reliability at the low target (ICC = 0.81, SEM = 10.2 mm). Normative data indicated greater repositioning errors at low targets in open-chain tasks and at high targets in closed-chain tasks. Correlations between open- and closed-chain errors were weak to absent. Open-chain JPS testing demonstrated acceptable reliability, whereas closed-chain reliability was dependent on target height. The two tasks appear to assess distinct aspects of proprioception. The open-chain test reflects predominantly single-joint (glenohumeral) position sense, whereas the closed-chain test reflects multi-joint, composite position sense. These findings establish initial reference values for JPS in male contact athletes.
