title: The Sleep and Diet of Elite Female Australian Rules Football Athletes Differ With Age and Season Phase.
abstract: The Australian Football League Women's (AFLW) competition is comprised of a short, intensive competitive season, highlighting the importance of proper fuelling and recovery to support performance. Little is known about the dietary and sleep habits of AFLW athletes across a season, and the influence that age has on these behaviours. Therefore, this study aimed to determine the effects of season phase and age on dietary intake and sleep in elite AFLW athletes. Dietary intake and sleep were assessed in 22 AFLW athletes (25.9 ± 5.0 y) over 10 nights, including five consecutive nights during both pre-season and in-season. Dietary intake was quantified through self-reported food diaries using a smartphone application (Easy Diet Diary), and sleep via a wearable monitoring device (Oura ring). Restricted maximum likelihood mixed models were used to determine variations in dietary intake and sleep in AFLW players between season phases (i.e., pre-season vs. in-season) and age. In-season protein (115.15 ± 35.14 vs. 126.48 ± 40.10 g, p = 0.026) and fat intakes (72.93 ± 29.55 vs. 83.43 ± 33.14 g, p = 0.012) were significantly lower compared to pre-season, with no differences in sleep measures observed between season phases. While age did not influence dietary intake, each additional year of age was associated with 8 min less sleep (p = 0.001) and 4 min earlier wake times (p = 0.032). These findings suggest that protein and fat intakes fluctuate across the seasons, with increasing age being a non-modifiable risk factor for shorter sleep durations within AFLW athletes.

title: Articular Cartilage-Derived Extracellular Matrix Material Promotes a Pro-Regenerative Macrophage Phenotype to Support Chondrogenesis.
abstract: Articular cartilage (AC) repair remains a major clinical challenge due to its limited healing capacity and the inability of current treatment strategies to restore long-term function. Biomaterial-based strategies which support favorable immune responses and appropriate progenitor cell function have shown promise in enhancing cartilage regeneration. We and others have previously demonstrated the capacity of extracellular matrix (ECM)-based materials to direct both innate immune cell behavior and progenitor cell differentiation, with these effects highly dependent on the ECM tissue of origin. Building on these observations, we now aim to further investigate the immunomodulatory properties of AC-derived ECM (AC-ECM) materials. Using primary human macrophages, we demonstrate that AC-ECM material promotes a metabolically active mixed response in macrophages, with elevated expression of reparative growth factors conducive to chondrogenesis. Furthermore, AC-ECM limits inflammatory activation of primary human macrophages, as demonstrated by reduced metabolic reprogramming and inflammatory cytokine production. Functionally, macrophages treated with AC-ECM enhance cartilage regeneration by increasing chondrogenic marker expression in mesenchymal stem cells, while also suppressing angiogenic tube formation in endothelial cells. Overall, this work demonstrates that AC-ECM biomaterials can direct macrophage phenotype toward a pro-chondrogenic state, offering a promising strategy for the development of more effective and durable cartilage repair therapies.

title: 660 nm LED preconditioning programs mitochondrial signaling in BMSCs for functional tracheal cartilage regeneration.
abstract: Stem-cell-based cartilage regeneration is limited not only by cell delivery, but also by the difficulty of establishing a stable and functionally competent regenerative cell state before implantation. Here, we report a photonic mitochondrial programming strategy in which 660 nm light-emitting diode (LED) irradiation preconditions bone marrow-derived mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs) to enhance functional tracheal cartilage regeneration. BMSCs were seeded onto egg white-derived ring-shaped porous scaffolds and exposed to defined 660 nm LED irradiation before implantation. Among the tested irradiation conditions, 15 J/cm2 optimally promoted BMSC proliferation, chondrogenic differentiation and cartilage-like extracellular matrix deposition, while suppressing fibrotic, hypertrophic and matrix-degrading phenotypes. Mechanistically, 660 nm LED irradiation enhanced cytochrome c oxidase (CCO) activity, mitochondrial membrane potential, adenosine triphosphate (ATP) production and respiratory function, accompanied by moderate reactive oxygen species (ROS) signaling. This mitochondrial bioenergetic-redox response activated the PI3K/Akt/mTOR/GSK3β-SOX9 axis, thereby promoting type II collagen, aggrecan and glycosaminoglycan-rich matrix formation. Pharmacological inhibition of ROS signaling, mitochondrial activity, PI3K or mTOR attenuated the LED-induced chondrogenic program. In a rabbit tracheal cartilage ring defect model, 15 J/cm2-preconditioned BMSC-scaffold constructs improved cartilage-like tissue formation, airway epithelial repair, lumen patency and mechanical support after 30 days of observation. These findings support 660 nm LED irradiation as a controllable mitochondrial preconditioning strategy for stem-cell-based functional cartilage regeneration.

title: Clonal articular cartilage progenitors outperform mesenchymal stromal cells in mitigating post-traumatic osteoarthritis.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to compare the functional, pathological, and immunomodulatory properties of articular chondroprogenitors (ACPs) with those of bone-marrow-derived mesenchymal stromal cells (MSCs) in preventing the progression of post-traumatic osteoarthritis (PTOA) after destabilization of the medial meniscus (DMM) injury in a mouse model.
METHOD: ACP and MSC were isolated from three horses and assessed for their immunomodulatory capacity in vitro. Aliquots of selected ACP clones and MSCs were injected intra-articularly into male mice 1-week post destabilization of the medial meniscus (DMM). The functional mobility of the mice before the injury and at weeks 2, 4, and 8 post-injury was assessed by two methods: ANY-maze™ voluntary mobility monitoring and DigiGait™ compulsory gait analysis. Upon euthanasia, joints were collected for histological scoring.
RESULTS: In vitro assessments demonstrated that ACPs and MSCs had anti-inflammatory properties: both treatments produced lower levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines, while only the ACPs produced more anti-inflammatory cytokines than controls. In vivo, both ACPs and MSCs lessened the effects of DMM on mobility. Histological scoring revealed significant reductions of PTOA in the medial compartment with ACPs relative to both MSCs and vehicle controls. Overall, ACPs effectively reduced PTOA progression to a greater extent than MSCs.
CONCLUSION: Our findings demonstrated that both equine ACP and MSC treatments provided symptom modification over vehicle controls in a short-term animal study. Notably, ACPs may be more efficacious than MSCs at reducing structural joint pathology.

title: Editorial Commentary: High Failure Rate of All-Inside Hamstring Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction at Long-Term Follow-Up: It's the Graft Not the Construct, but the Future Keeps Complicating the Past.
abstract: Recent reports of high failure rates after all-inside hamstring autograft anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction have renewed an old debate: is the problem the graft, the construct, or both? Interpretation is difficult because hamstring anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction has evolved alongside changes in graft configuration, socket drilling, and adjustable-loop cortical fixation. Potential contributors include graft elongation, unequal strand loading, adjustable-loop lengthening, and the longer working length of cortical fixation. Yet higher revision rates with hamstring autografts were identified before widespread adoption of the modern all-inside technique, suggesting that fixation alone does not explain the signal. Meanwhile, all-inside techniques have increasingly been paired with quadriceps tendon autograft without the same apparent failure concern. The literature remains messy, but the simplest explanation may still be the correct one: hamstring autograft itself appears less forgiving in higher-risk patients. For those patients, quadriceps or patellar tendon autograft remains the more reliable choice.

title: Cartilage-targeting engineered probiotic bacterial extracellular vesicles treat osteoarthritis through modulation of matrix homeostasis.
abstract: Reversing extracellular matrix (ECM) metabolic dysregulation to facilitate cartilage repair represents a key therapeutic strategy for osteoarthritis (OA) treatment. Owing to the avascular nature of joint structures, intra-articular injection is a commonly used clinical administration route. However, the current drug retention time is insufficient to effectively reverse OA progression. In this study, we demonstrated that natural bacterial extracellular vesicles (BEVs) are capable of repairing cartilage damage. We modified Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG (LGG)-derived BEVs with a chondrocyte-targeting peptide to prolong their therapeutic efficacy. Engineered BEVs, as a drug delivery system, are capable of continuously transporting endogenous miRNAs. Cartilage-targeting LGG-EVs (W-LGG-EVs) penetrate deeply into cartilage tissue and promote extracellular matrix secretion by chondrocytes. Furthermore, W-LGG-EVs were shown to restore cartilage homeostasis and ultimately alleviate stress-related OA. BEVs, as a novel and safe therapeutic agent, hold clinical feasibility.

title: The Influence of Sleep and Autonomic Recovery on Performance in World-Class Swimmers at Major Competitions: The Qualifying Trials, World Championships, and Olympic Games.
abstract: Sleep deprivation is one of the main risk factors for impaired performance in elite athletes, but the changes in sleep and autonomic regulation in response to competitions of varying levels within the same Olympic year remain unknown. In this prospective, longitudinal, observational study, we monitored parameters related to sleep quality and quantity, as well as heart rate variability and resting heart rate, in a cohort of eight Olympic swimmers (n = 8) during the World Championships in Doha, the qualifying trials, and the 2024 Paris Olympic Games, using the Oura Ring Gen3 under real-world conditions throughout the pre-competition, competition, and post-competition phases of each event. The Olympic Games were the only event where sleep efficiency fell below the commonly used reference threshold of 85% during the competition phase accompanied by a reduction in the total sleep score and an increase in resting heart rate. The Olympic setting was accompanied by temporary changes in sleep and autonomic markers, but no sleep parameter or autonomic marker showed a statistically significant association with intra-individual competitive performance, although the limited sample size constrains the power to detect such relationships.

title: Multidimensional Pre-Competition Stress Profiles in Wheelchair Basketball: Associations with Cortisol and Psychological Indicators.
abstract: This study examined pre-competition cortisol levels and psychological anticipation in wheelchair basketball athletes using a person-centred approach. Thirty-four male athletes (mean age: 35 ± 7.75 years) competing in a regional league provided saliva samples 35-50 min before competition and completed psychological assessments with the Revised Competitive State Anxiety Inventory-2 (CSAI-2R) and the Perceived Stress Scale. K-Means cluster analysis (k = 3), validated by Ward's hierarchical clustering (ARI = 0.947; NMI = 0.892) and Bootstrap Jaccard stability (0.544-0.603), identified three exploratory stress profiles: Low Reactor (n = 5; low cortisol, anxiety, and stress), High Reactor (n = 20; moderate cortisol, high cognitive/physical anxiety), and Physiological Stress Reactor (n = 9; high cortisol, high stress, moderate anxiety). Significant group differences were observed for log(Cortisol) (H(2) = 17.095, p < 0.001, ε2 = 0.518), Cognitive Anxiety (H(2) = 13.900, p < 0.01, ε2 = 0.421), Somatic Anxiety (H(2) = 18.840, p < 0.001, ε2 = 0.571), and Perceived Stress (H(2) = 21.831, p < 0.001, ε2 = 0.662), while self-confidence did not differ. Exploratory logistic regression indicated that functional classification, years of sport participation, match location, and match result did not significantly predict the Physiological Stress Reactor membership. These findings suggest that pre-competition stress-related characteristics may manifest in different combinations of physiological and psychological indicators. The identified profiles should be considered exploratory and require validation in larger and independent samples.

title: Long-Term Fitness Profile and Performance-Related Indicators in Semi-Professional Female Handball Players.
abstract: Long-term, single-club datasets linking fitness and match performance are rare in women's handball. This retrospective study profiled fitness and game-quality indicators across 14 seasons (2010-2022, 2026; N = 45; 8-17 players/season). Anthropometric and specific-fitness values (height 173.90 ± 5.53 cm, body mass 68.28 ± 8.08 kg, jump-throw velocity 79.94 ± 6.83 km/h, countermovement jump 43.46 ± 4.84 cm, VO2max 48.01 ± 3.61 mL/kg/min) were sub-elite. Shot efficiency (55.74 ± 6.00%) approached elite values (58.90 ± 7.60%). Backs were older, more experienced, and higher-scoring than Wings and Pivots. Universal players matched Backs' output despite being younger and less experienced. Experience correlated with goals per match (r = 0.51, p = 0.001), positive actions (r = 0.44, p = 0.005), and action balance (r = 0.47, p = 0.003). Throwing velocity and sprint/agility speed showed similar associations. Endurance, strength, and coordination/dribble deficit showed none. Fitness indicators improved across 2010-2022, but a single season after near-complete roster turnover departed markedly from this trend. Trends should not be extrapolated to a changed roster without retesting. A small set of trainable, sport-specific qualities, not general fitness, best predicts match performance. Findings provide normative benchmarks and training priorities for coaches.

title: The enhanced rehabilitation programme for significant musculoskeletal injuries from the manchester arena bombing - A process evaluation study investigating patients' and physiotherapists' experiences.
abstract: The 2017 Manchester Arena bombing exposed major gaps in the UK's civilian trauma rehabilitation services. In response, the Enhanced Rehabilitation after Major Trauma Programme (ERP), a structured, multidisciplinary rehabilitation approach, was developed by the NHS, in collaboration with the Universities of Manchester and Salford, and the Manchester Institute of Health and Performance (MIHP). This study employed the Normalisation Process Theory (NPT) framework to evaluate the integration and impact of ERP from the perspectives of physiotherapists and patients. Thirteen patients and four physiotherapists participated in semi-structured interviews and a focus group. Data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis (RTA) and then deductively with NPT constructs. Both groups regarded ERP as a valuable alternative to standard NHS rehabilitation. Its structured, multidisciplinary design supported physical and psychological recovery, improved motivation, and enhanced physiotherapist expertise. However, concerns were raised about sustaining progress after ERP, difficulties transitioning back to NHS care, and the absence of long-term rehabilitation pathways. Despite its positive outcomes, the wider adoption of ERP in the NHS faces barriers, including limited resources and systemic constraints. This study demonstrates the potential of structured rehabilitation models for trauma survivors. Future research should explore cost-effective ways to sustain and expand enhanced trauma rehabilitation.

title: Pre-season friendly match-play as a double-edged sword: Performance gains and inflammatory cost in semi-professional soccer players (a natural experiment).
abstract: Pre-season training prepares soccer players for competition, but the longitudinal effects of friendly match exposure remain unclear. We investigated whether cumulative late pre-season match-play is associated with physiological adaptation in semi-professional players. Twenty-four male players from a randomly selected semi-professional team competing at national level were assessed at pre-season start, mid-pre-season and pre-competition. Measurements included body composition, physical performance, aerobic fitness and blood markers reflecting muscle damage, inflammation, hormonal status and haematological adaptation. Based on cumulative playing time across eight friendly matches, as determined by coaching staff, players were classified retrospectively into extended play (EP) or limited play (LP) groups. Controlling for mid-pre-season baseline, the EP group showed significantly lower pre-competition values for body mass ( η p 2 = 0.276), body fat ( η p 2 = 0.294) and 35 m sprint time ( η p 2 = 0.129) and higher values for lower-limb power (dominant/non-dominant; η p 2 = 0.219-0.424), velocity at maximal oxygen uptake ( η p 2 = 0.441) and at second ventilatory threshold ( η p 2 = 0.708), serum glutamic-oxaloacetic transaminase ( η p 2 = 0.296), myoglobin ( η p 2 = 0.199), high-sensitivity C-reactive protein ( η p 2 = 0.920), interleukin-6 ( η p 2 = 0.893), tumour necrosis factor-α ( η p 2 = 0.937) and red blood cell count ( η p 2 = 0.190) (all P ≤ 0.038). Across all participants, total match-play time was correlated significantly with reductions in body fat (r = -0.47) and increases in lower-limb power (r = 0.44-0.67), second ventilatory threshold (r = 0.55) and inflammatory markers (r = 0.79-0.86) (all P ≤ 0.033). Greater friendly match-play exposure during pre-season was associated with favourable physiological adaptations and a more pronounced physiological and inflammatory response. These findings support friendly match-play as a meaningful physiological stimulus and highlight the importance of balancing match exposure with recovery during pre-season preparation.

title: Intensity-dependent microcurrent stimulation enhances BMSC-derived cartilage microtissue formation under defined culture conditions.
abstract: Engineering phenotypically favorable cartilage-like tissue from bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs) remains challenging because chondrogenic differentiation can be accompanied by insufficient cartilage-associated extracellular matrix accumulation and unfavorable hypertrophic and catabolic responses. Here, we established a microcurrent-assisted culture system for scaffold-free BMSC-derived cartilage microtissues (CMTs) and investigated the intensity-dependent effects of continuous unidirectional direct-current stimulation at 0, 50, 100, 150, 250, or 500 μA under a defined electrical and culture configuration. Among the tested conditions, 150 μA (nominal electrode current density, 3 μA/mm2) showed the most consistently favorable overall response, with enhanced cartilage-associated gene and protein expression, greater type II collagen- and glycosaminoglycan-rich matrix accumulation, improved CMT morphology, and higher apparent mechanical properties. In contrast, 250 and 500 μA were associated with reduced cartilage-associated matrix formation and increased fibrotic, hypertrophic, catabolic, inflammatory, and apoptosis-related markers. The 150 μA condition was also associated with a distinct intracellular Ca2+ response pattern and increased NFATc1 nuclear localization; verapamil, BAPTA-AM, and cyclosporin A attenuated NFATc1 nuclear localization, supporting involvement of Ca2+/calcineurin/NFAT-related signaling without establishing a unique causal mechanism. After 2 weeks of xenogeneic subcutaneous implantation in nude mice, CMTs preconditioned at 150 μA exhibited greater cartilage-like matrix accumulation and higher apparent compressive properties than those preconditioned at 0 or 500 μA. These findings identify 150 μA as the best-performing tested condition under the present electrical configuration and provide short-term ectopic proof-of-concept evidence, while longer-term orthotopic studies are required to evaluate phenotypic stability, tissue integration, and functional outcomes in cartilage-defect models.

title: Relationships Between Isometric Belt Squat Force and Vertical Jump Performance Across Knee Joint Angles.
abstract: Rebelo, A, Ripley, N, Weakley, J, and Comfort, P. Relationships between isometric belt squat force and vertical jump performance across knee joint angles. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-The aim of this study was to examine the relationships between vertical jump performance and isometric belt squat force assessed at 2 knee joint angles (120° and 90°) and to compare outcomes across age groups in male and female athletes. One hundred and twenty subjects (20.3 ± 6.5 years, 1.77 ± 0.12 m, 71.0 ± 13.3 kg) performed countermovement jumps, squat jumps, and isometric belt squat tests at 120° and 90° on dual force platforms. Between-group differences were analyzed using 1-way or Welch's analysis of variance with Bonferroni-adjusted post hoc analyses. Associations were examined using Pearson's correlations with Bonferroni-adjusted significance thresholds (p < 0.002), while omnibus tests used corrected alpha levels where applicable. Isometric belt squat net peak force demonstrated weak-to-moderate associations with jump height across tasks (r = 0.36-0.55). Associations between net force at 200 milliseconds and jump height were moderate at 90° (r = 0.45-0.52), whereas net force at 100 milliseconds showed negligible associations to jump height. Older athletes produced significantly higher absolute isometric net peak force than younger groups only at 90° knee flexion (up to ∼860 N difference), with moderate-to-large effects (g = 0.67-0.80), whereas relative net peak force did not differ between age categories. These findings indicate that the isometric belt squat can be confidently used to monitor maximal lower-limb force capacity across knee angles, with the 90° position offering greater sensitivity for distinguishing strength levels between age groups.

title: Use of 2.5% polyacrylamide hydrogel mitigates joint capsule stiffness and cartilage degradation in experimental equine osteoarthritis.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the symptom- and disease-modifying effects of injectable 2.5% polyacrylamide gel (iPAAG) in an experimental model of equine osteoarthritis (OA).
METHODS: 16 horses underwent osteochondral fragment creation (day 0) in 1 randomly-selected middle carpal joint (MCJ). On day 14, the MCJ was injected with 2 mL of phosphate-buffered saline (n = 8) or 2.5% iPAAG (8); high-speed treadmill exercise commenced on day 16 to induce OA. Clinical parameters (lameness, joint effusion, range of motion, flexion response) and synovial fluid were collected weekly and biweekly, respectively. Radiographs were obtained before surgery, at day 14, and at day 70. Postmortem evaluation (day 70) included gross, arthroscopic, and histopathologic evaluation of the MCJs and measurement of joint capsule stiffness.
RESULTS: There were no significant differences in clinical parameters or endpoint arthroscopic, macroscopic, or synovial membrane histopathology scores between groups. In 2.5% iPAAG-treated limbs, the third carpal bone had significantly lower (better) total articular cartilage histology scores (6.38 ± 4.10 vs 11.25 ± 4.20) and proteoglycan staining scores of the intermediate articular cartilage layer (0.38 ± 0.74 vs 1.88 ± 1.25) compared to saline-treated OA joints. Saline-treated OA joints had significantly increased joint capsule stiffness versus contralateral sham-operated MCJs (1,824 ± 1,105 vs 1,002 ± 495 Pa), whereas 2.5% iPAAG-treated joints did not (1,099 ± 647 vs 1,184 ± 504 Pa).
CONCLUSIONS: Treatment with 2.5% iPAAG showed some ability to mitigate the negative effects of OA on articular cartilage. Treatment also resulted in retention of normal joint capsule elasticity during the progression of OA.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Treatment with 2.5% iPAAG may result in retention of normal joint capsule elasticity in horses with naturally occurring OA.

title: Extracellular vesicles: Multi-source regulatory mechanisms in hippocampal homeostasis.
abstract: Hippocampal health is pivotal for memory, emotional regulation, and cognition. Extracellular vesicles (EVs) facilitate intercellular and inter-organ communication by transporting bioactive cargos; however, traditional research often overlooks systemic influences on the hippocampus in favor of local microenvironmental changes. This review synthesizes evidence demonstrating that hippocampal homeostasis is modulated by the organism's systemic state-including aging, obesity, and immune status-via EVs. We detail mechanisms by which EVs from peripheral organs (adipose tissue, gut/microbiota, lung, bone, muscle, liver, kidney, heart, and spleen) and central nervous system resident cells (neurons, microglia, astrocytes, neural stem cells, and endothelial cells) regulate hippocampal function. These multi-source EVs precisely modulate neurogenesis, inflammatory responses, and synaptic plasticity. Furthermore, we highlight the emerging role of migrasomes as a specialized subset of EVs in this regulatory landscape. By mapping this comprehensive EV-mediated network, we provide a holistic perspective on the crosstalk between the systemic environment and the hippocampus, offering novel insights and therapeutic strategies for diseases associated with hippocampal dysfunction.

title: PTHrP suppresses BMP2-induced osteochondral differentiation and preserves cartilage phenotype in mesenchymal stem cells via inactivating PI3K-AKT signaling.
abstract: Bone morphogenetic protein 2 (BMP2) has the potential to drive multipotent mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) to undergo chondral-osteogenic (including hypertrophic chondrocyte) differentiation. Parathyroid hormone-related protein (PTHrP) plays an essential role in fetal endochondral ossification, although persistent PTHrP stimulation leads to postnatal bone loss. Here, we investigated the effects of PTHrP on BMP2-induced endochondral ossification through hypertrophic chondrocyte differentiation of MSCs. We found that silencing PTHrP expression inhibited BMP2-induced chondrogenic, hypertrophic, and osteogenic differentiation of MSCs, while overexpression of PTHrP promoted BMP2-induced chondrogenic differentiation of MSCs and suppressed BMP2-induced hypertrophic differentiation of MSCs. Using stem cell implantation studies in athymic nude mice, we demonstrated that while MSCs with silenced PTHrP expression exhibited significantly reduced endochondral ossification of subcutaneous cartilage, overexpression of PTHrP promoted the growth of subcutaneous cartilage while significantly delaying ossification, leading to the preservation of cartilage phenotype. Mechanistically, we showed that exogenous PTHrP promoted BMP2-induced chondrogenic differentiation of MSCs by up-regulating Sox9 expression and inactivating PI3K-AKT signaling. Collectively, our findings strongly suggest that PTHrP may play an important role in mediating BMP2-induced chondral-osteogenic differentiation of MSCs by inactivating PI3K-AKT signaling, indicating that PTHrP may be exploited for endochondral cartilage-bone tissue engineering.

title: Targeting the lactate/P300/H3K18la epigenetic pathway with a mechanoadaptive biomimetic hydrogel to suppress traumatic tendon heterotopic ossification.
abstract: Traumatic heterotopic ossification (HO) is a debilitating complication of tendon injury, yet its pathogenic mechanisms remain elusive and effective preventive strategies are lacking. Here, we identify a glycometabolic-epigenetic axis that drives HO progression. Single-cell profiling and functional analyses reveal that hypoxic chondrocytes undergo glycolytic reprogramming, leading to lactate accumulation and transfer into tendon-derived mesenchymal stem cells (TD-MSCs) through MCT1. This metabolic coupling promotes P300-dependent histone H3 lysine 18 lactylation (H3K18la), activating osteogenic programs characterized by Col6a1, Zhx3, Lox and Vdr expression and thereby facilitating pathological endochondral ossification. Guided by this mechanism, we develop a tendon-adhesive hydrogel (GelHA-A485@Exos) that integrates mechanical repair with targeted epigenetic modulation. MSC-derived exosomes enable localized delivery of the P300 inhibitor A485, suppressing H3K18la and aberrant osteogenic activation, while the hydrogel scaffold enhances tendon regeneration. In vivo and in vitro studies demonstrate that GelHA-A485@Exos promotes tendon healing while preventing HO formation. Our findings establish metabolic-epigenetic communication as a central regulator of traumatic HO and provide a translational therapeutic strategy for its clinical prevention.

title: Mesenchymal stem/stromal cells and regenerative medicine.
abstract: Mesenchymal stem/stromal cells (MSCs) continue to drive innovation in regenerative medicine, yet the field is undergoing a critical evolution from the early concept of cellular engraftment to complex paracrine-mediated tissue repair. This review systematically evaluates the core scientific questions defining this transition, highlighting the latest advancements in MSC biology and the rapidly expanding therapeutic frontier of MSC-derived extracellular vesicles (MSC-EVs). We critically appraise recent progress in decoding MSC therapeutic mechanisms, specifically their profound capacity for immune modulation and microenvironmental remodeling. By synthesizing current findings across diverse and challenging clinical applications-encompassing oral tissue regeneration, osteoarthritis, and complex immune disorders-we provide expert insights into the discrepancies between promising preclinical data and variable clinical outcomes. Crucially, we address persistent translational bottlenecks, including inherent donor heterogeneity, manufacturing scalability, and the lack of standardized potency assays. It is our perspective that overcoming these limitations demands a strategic pivot towards precise cell-free MSC-EV therapies and advanced bioengineering strategies. Ultimately, this review highlights key directions for future research. By connecting basic mechanistic insights with clinical demands, we aim to accelerate the translation of effective MSC-based therapies.

title: Sleep, Chronotype and Physiological Acclimatisation During a 21-Day Altitude Training Camp in World-Class Swimmers.
abstract: Altitude training is widely used in elite swimming, although its effects on sleep and acclimatisation remain insufficiently understood. The aim of this study was to describe changes in sleep difficulty, physiological acclimatisation, athlete-reported outcomes, and haematological markers during a 21-day altitude training camp (2320 m), and to explore the association between chronotype and sleep difficulty. Seven world-class swimmers (4 men, 3 women) were monitored before, during, and after altitude exposure. Sleep difficulty was assessed using the Athlete Sleep Screening Questionnaire, while daily monitoring included resting oxygen saturation, resting heart rate, acute mountain sickness symptoms, fatigue, recovery, hydration status, and training load. Chronotype was determined using the Morningness-Eveningness Questionnaire. Sleep difficulty was descriptively higher during the first week at altitude (6.14 ± 1.07 vs. 4.14 ± 1.21 at baseline) and returned towards baseline by week 3 (4.29 ± 1.50), although pairwise comparisons did not remain significant after multiplicity correction. Strong inverse associations between chronotype and sleep difficulty were observed at baseline (rho = -0.87, p = 0.014) and week 1 (rho = -0.85, p = 0.019), but neither met the Bonferroni-adjusted significance threshold (α = 0.010). SpO2 increased across the camp, with week 3 significantly higher than weeks 1 and 2 after Bonferroni correction, whereas RHR was significantly lower in week 3 than in week 1, but not week 2, after correction. Athlete-reported outcomes remained stable, acute mountain sickness symptoms were minimal, and haematological and iron-status markers showed no significant pre-to-post changes. Sleep difficulty showed a transient descriptive increase during the initial phase of the altitude camp, while SpO2 and RHR changes were consistent with physiological acclimatisation. Chronotype-related differences in sleep difficulty appeared to be present before altitude exposure rather than emerging specifically during the camp. Given the small sample size, these findings should be considered exploratory and hypothesis-generating.

title: Limb Ischemia-Reperfusion Injury in Rats is partially mediated by enhancing Necroptosis via Phosphorylation of RIPK1 and MLKL.
abstract: Limb ischemia-reperfusion injury (L-IRI) causes severe skeletal muscle damage and functional impairment through activation of regulated cell-death and inflammatory pathways. Necroptosis is a regulated form of necrotic cell death mediated through the receptor-interacting protein kinase 1 (RIPK1)-RIPK3-mixed lineage kinase domain-like protein (MLKL) signaling axis. Prior experimental studies have shown that Necrostatin-1 (Nec-1) attenuates acute skeletal muscle ischemia-reperfusion injury in rats. However, how Nec-1-sensitive protection relates to RIPK1/MLKL-associated signaling, circulating muscle injury markers, inflammatory responses, histological damage, and functional recovery during the early postischemic period remains incompletely defined. In this study, we used a rat model of unilateral hindlimb ischemia involving 3 hours of ischemia followed by reperfusion for up to 7 days to evaluate these interrelated responses. Nec-1 was administered before ischemia and after reperfusion. L-IRI resulted in elevated plasma creatine kinase and lactate dehydrogenase levels, severe histopathological injury, increased TUNEL staining, impaired grip strength, and reduced Modified Tarlov scores. These changes were accompanied by increased phosphorylation of RIPK1 and MLKL, activation of inflammatory signaling pathways, and altered expression of injury-associated inflammatory mediators. Nec-1 treatment reduced RIPK1/MLKL-associated signaling, inflammatory mediator expression, circulating muscle injury markers, and histological injury while preserving muscle architecture and improving functional recovery. These findings support and extend previous evidence that Nec-1-sensitive necroptosis-associated signaling contributes to early skeletal muscle injury following L-IRI. Pharmacologic targeting of regulated necrotic and inflammatory pathways warrants further investigation as a potential adjunct strategy for limiting acute skeletal muscle injury after limb reperfusion.

title: Mechanobiology in Osteoarthritis: From Crosstalk of Mechanosensitive Signaling Pathways to the Intervention Mechanisms and Therapeutic Potential of Exercise.
abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) is the most prevalent joint degeneration globally. Once considered passive "wear and tear", it is now recognized as a metabolically active, whole-joint disease driven by genetic, metabolic, inflammatory, and mechanical factors. The core pathology is failed mechanotransduction, where a dysregulated mechanosensitive signaling network disrupts joint homeostasis, causing cartilage degradation, synovitis, and pain. This review re-examines OA pathogenesis through network biology, highlighting that OA stems from the dysregulation of a complex mechanosensitive network-including Piezo, Transient Receptor Potential Vanilloid 4 (TRPV4), Integrin-Focal Adhesion Kinase (integrin-FAK), Hippo/yes-associated protein-transcriptional coactivator with PDZ-binding motif (Hippo/YAP-TAZ), and Wingless/Integrated /β-catenin (Wnt/β-catenin) pathways. These pathways engage in extensive crosstalk via shared secondary messengers (calcium ions, reactive oxygen species) to determine cell fate. Furthermore, exercise acts as a physiological "mechanotherapy" to recalibrate this network, shifting cellular responses from catabolic/inflammatory states to anabolic/homeostatic ones. We also explore the translational potential of restoring network balance using precision mechanotherapy, advanced drug delivery, and biomaterials. OA is fundamentally a systemic network failure from failed mechanotransduction. Future therapies should shift from single-target interventions to systemic reprogramming of the dysregulated network. Utilizing biomaterials, smart drug delivery, and personalized exercise can advance OA management from symptomatic relief to active tissue regeneration and disease reversal.

title: Shallow under load? Prevalence of acetabular morphologies and their association with sport exposure during skeletal maturation in professional female football players: a retrospective study using data from the PROFE cohort.
abstract: We aimed to report the prevalence of acetabular morphologies in professional female footballers and explore the association between these morphologies and sport exposure during the period of skeletal maturation. 100 professional female footballers (200 hips) were included. Athletes with a history of systemic disease were excluded. Questionnaires obtained information on previous sport frequencies and age of menarche. Participants reported the minimum hours of sport played weekly during three age categories/stages of growth: cartilaginous hypertrophy (8-10 years), skeletal growth (11-12 years), and closure of growth plates (13-16 years). Participants underwent a pelvic radiograph. The Wiberg-center edge angle classified hips with normal coverage, borderline dysplasia, dysplasia or pincer morphology. Logistic regression models explored the association between prevalence of acetabular morphologies and minimum of sport hours played weekly in different age groups. Interactions with age of menarche were explored. From 200 hips, 32% were classified as having borderline dysplasia, 9% had dysplasia, 1% had pincer morphology, and 58% had normal coverage. Athletes with a later age of menarche had higher odds of dysplasia with increasing sport exposure between 8-10 (OR [95%CI] = 1.23 [1.05-1.44]). p = 0.011) and 11-12 years (OR [95%CI] = 1.21 [1.06-1.38], p = 0.006) compared to those with an earlier age of menarche. Skeletal maturation might be an important period for the development of acetabular morphology in female footballers. Exposure to high‑load sport activity during skeletal maturation and age of menarche may contribute to the development of hip dysplasia in these athletes.

title: Metabolic Bone Health in Female Patients: Focus on Foot and Ankle.
abstract: Metabolic bone health is crucial for the overall well-being of female patients. Female athletes and young females are of particular interest, as their skeletal systems are still developing and are sensitive to the hormonal and physical stress of training and diet. Stress fractures occur with higher frequency in females with risk factors such as low bone mineral density (BMD). When low bone mineral density occurs along with menstrual irregularities and relative energy deficiency, it completes the female triad (23, 27, and 28). Any discussion of female BMD and metabolic bone health must include the female triad.

title: EMSCs-derived exosomes rescue p75NTR-/- -mediated osteogenesis deficiency via PI3K/Akt/ERK1/2 signaling pathways.
abstract: The repair of the critical-sized bone defects remains a major challenge for orthopedic surgeons, particularly when osteogenesis is impaired by p75 neurotrophin receptor (p75NTR) deficiency. However, the underlying molecular mechanisms are not fully understood. This study aimed to clarify the role of p75NTR in bone regeneration and to develop a cell-free approach to rescue p75NTR-/- deficiency-mediated osteogenic deficiency through a controlled releasing of wild-type ectomesenchymal stem cells exosomes (WT-Exo) which were incorporated into silk fibroin/polycaprolactone2:5/polyvinyl alcohol (SF/PCL2:5/PVA) coaxial nanofibrous membranes. p75NTR-/- mice exhibited a reduced bone mass and delayed ossification, while WT-Exo-loaded membranes partially restored osteogenic deficiency in p75NTR-/- cells and enhanced expression of osteogenic markers such as alkaline phosphatase (ALP), collagen type I (Col-I), osteopontin (OPN) and runt-related transcription factor 2 (Runx2) aaccompanied by activating of phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K)/protein kinase B (Akt)/extracellular signal-regulated kinase 1/2 (ERK1/2) signaling pathway. Following implantation of the WT-Exo-loaded membranes into the critical-sized cranial defects in p75NTR-/- mice, new bone formation in the defect site was significantly improved by a sustained release of WT-Exo. Overall, the findings in this study highlighted the critical role of p75NTR in osteogenic differentiation of ectomesenchymal stem cells (EMSCs) and demonstrated that WT-Exo, delivered via the coaxial electrospun membranes, represented an effective cell-free intervention method to reverse bone formation deficiency caused by p75NTR deficiency, providing a promising strategy for gene deficiency-related bone diseases.

title: Advancing regenerative biomaterials and translational strategies in orthopaedic traumatology.
abstract: The 2025 Orthopaedic Trauma Association's Basic Science Focus Forum featured a symposium on regenerative biomaterials and translational strategies for orthopaedic trauma. Four experts presented complementary perspectives on the next generation of bone and soft tissue repair: Dr. J. Tracy Watson described how orthobiologics and refined spacer design can be used to engineer a better Masquelet induced membrane; Dr. Lauren Priddy presented evidence that hydroxyapatite coatings can mitigate the rapid degradation of additively manufactured magnesium scaffolds; Dr. Vaida Glatt described the development and clinical translation of the Biomimetic Hematoma scaffold for bone and muscle regeneration; and Dr. Katherine Hixon outlined how the 3R principles (Replacement, Reduction, Refinement) can serve as a framework to accelerate musculoskeletal regenerative engineering. Collectively, the symposium underscored a shift toward biologically informed, clinically predictive, and ethically responsible engineering solutions for the patients who sustain musculoskeletal trauma.

title: Supporting adolescent menstrual health to improve participation and performance in physical activity: rapid realist review to inform a logic model for intervention development.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Insufficient physical activity is higher in women and girls globally, with increased risk of non-communicable diseases. Menstrual (period-related) symptoms are a recognised barrier to adolescents engaging in physical activity. There is a lack of evidence-based guidance to address this barrier.
OBJECTIVE: To develop a set of initial programme theories (context-mechanism-outcome configurations, CMOCs) to describe how existing menstrual health support interventions work, for whom, how and in what circumstances to inform a logic model for intervention development.
DESIGN: Rapid realist review.
METHODS: Formal, double-screened, database (Medline, AMED, Embase, Psycinfo, CINAHL, ERIC, SCOPUS; June 2025) and grey literature searches guided by stakeholder expertise. Articles were selected that met inclusion criteria and contributed to theory development. Explanatory statements were extracted and synthesised into CMOCs using Pawson’s reasoning processes and mapped onto Self-Determination Theory concepts (autonomy, competency, relatedness).
RESULTS: From 9585 database hits, 63 articles were included. Three generated initial programme theories describe how four identified intervention domains (education; practicalities including toilet facilities, clothing and free accessible period products; menstrual cycle tracking and screening tools; and medical support if needed) could improve menstrual health confidence and understanding (M), communication and trust (M)—to empower individuals to enhance their own menstrual health (M) and potentially improve participation rates and performance in physical activity (O). Alternative causal pathways describe potential adverse outcomes when processes are not in place to: signpost to medical support if needed (M), support user trust in how and why data are collected and used (M) and enable understanding of the limitations of menstrual health support tools (M). Contextual data are needed to further refine these theories that are presented as a logic model.
CONCLUSION: The proposed logic model can be used to inform and evaluate future interventions aimed at overcoming menstrual health related barriers with physical activity.

title: Young Investigator Award: Where Do We Start? A Conceptual Model for Implementing Menstrual Cycle Tracking in Sport.
abstract: Menstrual cycle tracking is a much-discussed component of the ' female athlete' research theme; however, more translational work is needed to meet practitioners' desire for further guidance on the implementation of tracking in applied settings. The purpose of this paper is to present a preliminary conceptual model to inform practitioners' decision-making around menstrual cycle tracking and assist researchers in identifying and framing future research directions. The proposed model-Conducting and Navigating menstrual cycle Education, Communication and Tracking (ConNECT)-proposes that communication and education strategies may be utilised to affect social, organisational and individual level change, ultimately supporting the implementation of menstrual cycle tracking by increasing its uptake and impact. This model was developed based on the findings from a series of studies conducted by the authors, which considered the existing literature on tracking and the perspectives of athletes and practitioners. Therefore, the ConNECT model offers an ecologically sound starting point for sport scientists, coaches and other members of an athlete's support team to base their practice on.

title: Baseline Symptom Collection in Elite Rugby Union Players-Limited Clinical Utility? An Investigation of Assessments Across 5879 men and Women Athletes.
abstract: In World Rugby's Head Injury Assessment (HIA) protocol, a modified Sports Concussion Assessment Tool (SCAT) is completed during the pre-season (baseline) and when a player has a suspected head injury. The symptom component of the SCAT, which involves comparing current to baseline symptoms, has been shown to be the most predictive component for concussion diagnosis. Because the clinical comparison of symptom report to baseline is a key determinant of concussion diagnosis, this study aims to explore the relationship between symptoms endorsement at baseline and during HIA. Mean and standard deviation (SD) or median and interquartile ranges (IQR) are presented along with relevant bivariate analyses. Logistic regressions compared proportions of symptom endorsement profiles between men and women. At baseline, 'Trouble sleeping' and 'Fatigue or low energy' were commonly reported symptoms for men and women. At baseline, women (mean + SD) reported more symptoms than men (mean + SD) on average. During the HIA, women players were nearly 3 times (Relative risk: 2.98 95% CIs: 2.47-3.60) more likely than men to report fewer symptoms immediately after the match than at baseline (47% women vs. 16% men). While this study highlights the importance of collecting baseline assessment as a medical overview of players, it de-emphasises the relevance of baseline symptoms when using the SCAT as a clinical assessment tool in professional rugby players. This study also highlights important differences in men and women's rugby players in symptom reporting, and recommends de-coupling baseline symptom reporting from the diagnostic part of the HIA.

title: Varying Lateral Extra-articular Tenodesis Femoral Fixation Points and Fixation Flexion Angles Do Not Affect ACL Graft Force and Tibiofemoral Motion After ACL Reconstruction.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The addition of lateral extra-articular tenodesis (LET) to anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction (ACLR) has been shown to reduce rotational laxity and improve graft survivorship. Despite the increased utilization of LET with ACLR, there remains a lack of consensus on the ideal location of the femoral attachment site of LET.
PURPOSE: To compare ACL graft force and tibiofemoral motion in cadaveric specimens undergoing ACLR with the addition of LET at varying fixation angles and fixation points.
STUDY DESIGN: Controlled laboratory study.
METHODS: A total of 10 fresh-frozen cadaveric knees were tested in 6 conditions, including LET fixation at 2 anatomic locations. Location 1 was defined as 8 mm proximal and 4 to 5 mm posterior to the lateral femoral epicondyle, at the insertion of the anterolateral ligament. Location 2 was defined as 31 mm proximal to the lateral femoral epicondyle, at the insertion of the distal Kaplan fibers. The testing conditions were as follows: (1) native; (2) ACLR; (3) ACLR + LET at location 1, fixed at 30°; (4) ACLR + LET at location 2, fixed at 30°; (5) ACLR + LET at location 1, fixed at 60°; and (6) ACLR + LET at location 2, fixed at 60°. Specimens were mounted on a 6 degrees of freedom robotic system to assess tibial internal rotation and anterior tibial translation at 0°, 30°, 60°, and 90° of knee flexion. A load cell was utilized to assess ACL graft force.
RESULTS: There were no differences between the 4 LET states in any outcome. In internal rotation, the addition of LET demonstrated reductions in ACL graft force in all 4 configurations, ranging from -14.9 N (14%) to -19.5 N (20%) at 0°, -19.7 N (51%) to -21.4 N (55%) at 30°, and -3.9 N (30%) to -4.6 N (35%) at 60° (all P < .05). The addition of LET also demonstrated reductions in internal rotation range of motion in all 4 configurations, ranging from -1.86° (15%) to -2.45° (19%) at 0°, -4.87° (18%) to -5.75° (20%) at 30°, and -4.70° (19%) to -5.92° (23%) at 60° (all P < .05).
CONCLUSION: Variations in LET fixation location and fixation flexion angle did not alter its effect on ACL graft force reduction or tibiofemoral motion in the cadaveric knee. The addition of LET had a protective effect on the ACL graft in internal rotation while demonstrating overconstraint compared to the native knee.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: The findings suggest that surgeons may have flexibility in selecting the femoral fixation location and knee flexion angle for LET without substantially altering its biomechanical effect on ACL graft loading or tibiofemoral kinematics. However, because LET reduced internal rotation beyond the native state, care should be taken to avoid excessive constraint when performing the procedure.

title: Integration of dynamic apnea into routine coach-led training in competitive BMX riders: A controlled pilot study.
abstract: Dynamic apnea (DA) has been proposed as a conditioning strategy for high-intensity exercise, but its integration into routine BMX training has not been investigated. We examined the effects of an eight-week DA program integrated into coach-led BMX training. Nineteen competitive BMX riders entered the study; 12 completed the protocol (AG, n = 6; CG, n = 6). AG performed repeated apneas during selected cycling sections, while CG completed matched training without apnea. Sprint performance, heart-rate responses, maximal static apnea and post-exercise blood lactate were assessed before and after training. AG improved 300-m performance compared with CG (adjusted difference: -0.79 s; p = 0.017), whereas no significant between-group differences were observed for 500-m and start performance. Peak heart rate was lower in AG than CG after training during the 300-m and 500-m performances. Maximal static apnea increased, with a stronger and faster bradycardic response in AG than CG. Blood lactate did not differ significantly between groups, although four of six AG riders showed a marked reduction. Among protocol completers, DA was integrated into supervised routine BMX training and was associated with improved 300-m performance and cardiovascular adaptations. These preliminary findings require confirmation in larger cohorts.

title: DNA-adsorbing nanozyme hydrogel reprograms the immuno-oxidative microenvironment to support stem cell-based cartilage repair in osteoarthritis.
abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a prevalent degenerative joint disease, and stem cell therapy is often limited by a hostile joint microenvironment. Excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS) and damage-associated cell-free DNA (cfDNA) cooperatively drive innate immune activation, inflammatory macrophage polarization, and chondrogenic instability, forming an immuno-oxidative barrier to cartilage repair. Here, we developed a bioactive DNA-adsorbing nanozyme hydrogel (MNKB/HA) to remodel this niche and enhance BMSC-mediated cartilage repair. MNKB/HA integrates Mn3O4 nanozymes with Kartogenin (KGN)-engineered bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs) in an injectable hyaluronic acid matrix. Mn3O4 exhibited SOD- and CAT-like activities, scavenging O2·-, H2O2, and ·OH, while efficiently adsorbing cfDNA and CpG-ODN to suppress TLR9/MyD88 signaling and M1 polarization and promote M2 polarization. In vitro, 10 μg/mL Mn3O4 was cytocompatible, protected BMSCs and chondrocytes from H2O2-induced apoptosis, and reshaped inflammatory secretion, with IL-10 increased 8.3-fold and TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-1β reduced. KGN stabilized the chondrogenic phenotype (SOX9, COL Ⅱ, ACAN), while its combination with Mn3O4 synergistically enhanced chondrogenic stability under oxidative/inflammatory stress. In rat OA, intra-articular MNKB/HA reduced OARSI scores, restored COL II and ACAN, decreased MMP13, improved subchondral bone microarchitecture, and attenuated synovitis and osteophytes. MNKB/HA also reduced synovial cfDNA, weakened TLR9 signaling, promoted M2 polarization, and showed intra-articular retention for at least 10 days without notable systemic toxicity. Thus, MNKB/HA remodels the immuno-oxidative niche through synergistic ROS scavenging and cfDNA adsorption, providing a strategy for stem cell-mediated cartilage repair in OA.

title: M4-like Macrophages Drive Skeletal Muscle Fibrosis and Suppress Myogenesis via the MMP12/SPP1/NF-κB Axis.
abstract: Acute skeletal muscle repair depends on a finely tuned balance between myogenic regeneration and fibrotic remodeling. Macrophages are essential to this process, and specific subsets have been linked to fibrosis in some organs. The M4-like macrophage, a distinct polarization subset implicated in fibrotic diseases, has not been well characterized in the context of injured muscle, particularly regarding its impact on fibroblast activation and myogenic suppression. The study aims to explore the effects of M4-like macrophages in the repair of muscle injury and possible mechanism. We analyzed a murine single-cell RNA-sequencing dataset from cardiotoxin (CTX)-injured skeletal muscle to identify injury-expanded macrophage subsets and their molecular programs. Immunohistochemistry and immunofluorescence staining of muscle sections were used to assess CXCL4 expression and platelet (CD41+) infiltration in injured versus uninjured tissues. CXCL4-induced M4-like macrophages were established as an in vitro model to examine their effects on L929 fibroblasts and C2C12 myoblasts. The MMP12-SPP1 interaction was predicted by AlphaFold3 and validated by co-immunoprecipitation and immunofluorescence colocalization. Loss-of-function and rescue experiments targeting MMP12 and SPP1 were performed to determine their causal roles in fibroblast activation and myogenic suppression. Transcriptomic and biochemical analyses were used to define downstream macrophage-intrinsic NF-κB/TNF-α signaling. Finally, AAV-mediated macrophage-targeted SPP1 knockdown and pharmacological NF-κB inhibition were evaluated in the CTX injury model. Using a BALB/c mouse model of cardiotoxin (CTX)-induced acute skeletal muscle injury and a publicly available murine scRNA-seq dataset from CTX-injured skeletal muscle, we observed an injury-induced MMP12/SPP1-positive macrophage subset with an M4-like transcriptional signature. Mechanistically, co-immunoprecipitation assays and immunofluorescence colocalization supported an association between MMP12 and SPP1. MMP12 knockdown attenuated the pro-fibrotic and anti-myogenic effects of M4-like macrophages, whereas recombinant SPP1 largely restored these phenotypes. Furthermore, transcriptomic and biochemical analyses revealed that autocrine SPP1 activated NF-κB signaling in M4-like macrophages, and increased TNF-α secretion. Pharmacological inhibition of NF-κB signaling with QNZ reduced fibroblast activation and restored the expression of myogenic markers. However, QNZ is not TNF-α specific and may affect multiple cell types. In vivo, AAV-mediated macrophage-targeted SPP1 knockdown driven by the F4/80 promoter, as well as QNZ treatment in the CTX-induced muscle injury model, markedly decreased collagen deposition, enhanced myogenic regeneration, and improved functional recovery. These findings identify an MMP12/SPP1/NF-κB signaling pathway in M4-like macrophages, with TNF-α as a potential downstream mediator, that may contribute to an imbalance between regeneration and fibrosis and may represent a therapeutic target for enhancing skeletal muscle repair after acute injury.

title: Superiority of Tetrapeptide Tyr-Gly-Leu-Phe over Amino Acid Mixture: Mechanisms Underlying Enhanced Systemic Amino Acid Delivery, Anti-Fatigue Efficacy, and Muscle Damage Repair.
abstract: This study compared the anti-fatigue tetrapeptide YGLF with an equimolar amino acid (AA) mixture across three stages: postingestion absorption, postexercise fatigue, and muscle damage repair. Despite rapid in vitro degradation (<1% intact), YGLF elevated plasma AAs more effectively than the AA mixture 15 min postingestion (51.97 vs 46.34 mg/100 mL). Postexercise, YGLF outperformed the AA mixture by further increasing muscle AAs and blood glucose, reducing metabolic byproducts, and activating AMPK. Following muscle damage, transcriptomics revealed that the AA mixture primarily modulated energy metabolism, whereas YGLF uniquely upregulated muscle growth genes. Western blotting confirmed that YGLF promoted repair via the Sestrin2/mTOR and Pax7/MYOD pathways. These findings demonstrate the distinct bioactivity of YGLF over that of free AAs, establishing a rationale for utilizing specific peptides in sports nutrition and muscle recovery.

title: WNT5A-Associated Osteogenic Enhancement Contributes to the Protective Effects of OPG-Fc in Glucocorticoid-Associated Femoral Head Osteonecrosis.
abstract: Steroid-induced osteonecrosis of the femoral head (SONFH) is a progressive orthopedic disorder characterized by an imbalance between bone resorption and bone formation. Although receptor activator of nuclear factor kappa-B ligand (RANKL) blockers are known to suppress osteoclast activity, whether they also promote osteogenesis and the underlying molecular mechanisms remain poorly understood. In this study, we investigated whether osteoprotegerin-Fc (OPG-Fc) exerts osteoprotective effects in SONFH and whether wingless-type MMTV integration site family, member 5A (WNT5A) signaling is involved. A rat SONFH model was established using lipopolysaccharide (LPS) combined with methylprednisolone sodium succinate (MPS), and bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs) were cultured under glucocorticoid-containing conditions. OPG-Fc, the WNT5A antagonist box5, and Wnt5a knockdown were used, and analyses included micro-computed tomography (micro-CT), histological staining, transcriptome sequencing, quantitative reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR), and western blotting. Our results demonstrated that OPG-Fc significantly improved bone trabecular microarchitecture, reduced empty lacunae and tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase (TRAP)-positive cells, and increased cartilage thickness in vivo. In vitro, OPG-Fc promoted osteogenic differentiation while inhibiting adipogenic differentiation of BMSCs. Transcriptome and protein analyses revealed significantly higher WNT5A expression following OPG-Fc treatment. Importantly, pharmacological blockade of WNT5A with box5 and Wnt5a knockdown partially attenuated OPG-Fc-associated pro-osteogenic effects, whereas box5 had limited effects on anti-resorptive marker changes. These findings suggest that OPG-Fc exerts dual protective actions in SONFH by suppressing bone resorption and enhancing osteogenic differentiation in association with WNT5A-related signaling. This study provides new mechanistic insights into RANKL blockade therapy and offers a potential molecular target for early intervention in SONFH.

title: Delphinidin induces the upregulation of miR-23a-3p expression in skeletal muscle and miR-23a-3p release from intestinal cells.
abstract: Delphinidin, one of the major anthocyanidins, inhibits disuse muscle atrophy by increasing the expression of miR-23a-3p in mouse skeletal muscle. However, delphinidin is less stable and poorly absorbed in vivo, so its mechanism of function remains unclear. In this study, we aimed to elucidate the mechanism by which delphinidin increases miR-23a-3p expression in skeletal muscle. miRNAs can be packaged into extracellular vesicles (EVs) and secreted from cells. We investigated whether delphinidin induces the release of miR-23a-3p encapsulated in EVs from intestinal cells and whether these EVs increase miR-23a-3p expression in skeletal muscle cells. A single dose of delphinidin increased the expression of miR-23a-3p in the small intestine of mice. To examine whether delphinidin affects the secretion of miR-23a-3p in intestinal cells, we used differentiated Caco-2 cells as an in vitro model. Results showed that delphinidin increases the expression of miR-23a-3p in EVs secreted from differentiated Caco-2 cells. In addition, EVs derived from delphinidin-treated Caco-2 cells were taken up by differentiated C2C12 myotubes, resulting in increased intracellular miR-23a-3p expression. Our in vitro results suggest that intestinal cell-derived EVs may contribute to the antimuscle atrophy activity of delphinidin through the delivery of miR-23a-3p to skeletal muscle cells.

title: Myogenic differentiation-derived small extracellular vesicles as a therapeutic strategy for miR-193b-3p-mediated muscle regeneration.
abstract: The regeneration of skeletal muscle involves precisely regulated intercellular communication, including extracellular vesicle (EV)-mediated processes. In this study, we show that during in vitro myogenic differentiation of human skeletal muscle progenitor cells (myoblasts), miR-193b-3p accumulates within small EVs (sEVs) in a temporally regulated manner. Both sEV-mediated and synthetic delivery of miR-193b-3p enhanced myogenic differentiation in vitro and promoted histological recovery in a murine volumetric muscle loss model. Mechanistically, we demonstrate that miR-193b-3p directly suppresses adapter-related protein complex 2 subunit mu 1 (AP2M1), a clathrin-associated adapter protein that has not been well characterized in muscle biology, and identify it as a negative regulator of myogenic progression. AP2M1 knockdown phenocopied the effects of miR-193b-3p, suggesting that this regulatory axis may contribute to muscle regeneration. In addition, transcriptomic analyses of aged rodent and sarcopenic human datasets revealed conserved upregulation of AP2M1 in degenerative muscle states, supporting its potential clinical relevance. Collectively, these findings reveal a myogenic differentiation-dependent, sEV-mediated miRNA regulatory mechanism that contributes to muscle regeneration. Based on these results, we propose the miR-193b-3p-AP2M1 axis as a potential therapeutic target for muscle-wasting disorders.

title: Binding of a Novel 11β-Hydroxysteroid to the Apelin Receptor (APLNR) and Its Possible Role in Regulating Skeletal Muscle Health in Mice.
abstract: Several molecules have been investigated for their potential to improve muscle health in models of muscle damage simulating sarcopenia, injury, or aging. Some small molecules induced beneficial effects on skeletal muscle by stimulating the apelin receptor (APLNR). This receptor has emerged as a promising pharmacological target for modulating muscle homeostasis. Using an in silico approach, we recently identified 11β-hydroxypregnenolone (11β-OHP5) as a potential skeletal muscle (SKM) modulator. We hypothesized that 11β-OHP5 interacts with and activates APLNR. This study employed several research approaches: (1) in silico molecular docking and molecular dynamics to explore the feasibility of 11β-OHP5 interacting with APLNR; (2) in vitro activation analysis to APLNR; (3) in vitro analysis C2C12 myoblast differentiation; (4) analysis of the molecule's presence in mouse skeletal muscle and its differential presence between young and older mice. The results show that 11β-OHP5, acting through APLNR, positively affects myoblast differentiation and may participate in the exercise-induced benefits in aging mice. We show that 11β-OHP5 interacts with APLNR, induces myogenic responses, is found in SKM; its concentration decreases with age, and exercise restores it. More work is necessary to understand the physiology of this possible endogenous molecule.

title: Aerobic Exercise Ameliorates Osteoarthritic Chondrocyte Degradation in Osteoarthritis via Regulating E2F8/NLRP14 Signaling Pathway.
abstract: Although physical activity is known to mitigate disease risks, its protective molecular mechanisms remain poorly understood. E2F8, a regulator of cell cycle and metabolism, showed significant differential expression between osteoarthritis (OA) and exercise models, suggesting it may link mechanical activity to OA alleviation. In vitro, Interleukin-1 Beta (IL-1β) simulated inflammation. In vivo, OA was induced in rats via Monosodium iodoacetate (MIA) injection. The effects of E2F8 and mechanical stress were assessed using moderate treadmill exercise, histology, and joint observation. Bioinformatic analysis, cyclic tensile strain, Western blot, immunofluorescence, and gene knockdown were used to investigate mechanisms. In OA rats, E2F8 was downregulated in cartilage while NLRP14 increased. Exercise reversed E2F8 downregulation, alleviated cartilage degeneration, restored anabolic activity, and reduced inflammatory catabolism linked to senescence. In vitro, mechanical stress reversed the IL-1β-induced anabolic/catabolic imbalance by regulating the E2F8/NLRP14, mitigating OA progression. Mechanical stress enhances E2F8 expression in osteoarthritic chondrocytes, which in turn protects cartilage by suppressing the expression of NLRP14. These findings underscore the role of E2F8 as a mechano-sensitive mediator and highlight the potential of exercise or exercise-mimetic therapies as effective strategies for preventing and treating OA.

title: Chaenomeles speciosa-derived extracellular vesicles accelerate fracture healing via orchestrating immuno-angiogenic coupling.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Fracture nonunion remains a major orthopaedic challenge, and dysregulation of the bone immune microenvironment is increasingly recognized as a key pathological driver. Chaenomeles speciosa is a medicinal plant with documented anti-inflammatory properties, making it a promising candidate for immune-modulatory therapy. This study investigated whether extracellular vesicles derived from Chaenomeles speciosa could reshape the immune microenvironment to promote fracture healing.
METHODS: Single-cell RNA sequencing was performed on human nonunion tissues to characterize cellular heterogeneity. Network pharmacology and molecular docking analyses were used to identify potential therapeutic targets of Chaenomeles speciosa. Extracellular vesicles were isolated by ultracentrifugation and characterized by transmission electron microscopy. Macrophage polarization, angiogenesis, and inflammatory signaling were assessed in vitro using RAW 264.7 macrophages and human umbilical vein endothelial cells. Bone regeneration was evaluated in a rat femoral fracture model using micro-computed tomography and histology.
RESULTS: Single-cell RNA sequencing revealed M1 macrophage dominance and enhanced M1-mediated communication with osteoblasts and endothelial cells in nonunion tissues. The IL-17 signaling pathway and matrix metalloproteinase-3 were identified as key therapeutic targets. Isolated extracellular vesicles exhibited excellent biocompatibility, promoted M2 macrophage polarization, attenuated inflammation, and enhanced angiogenesis in vitro. In the rat fracture model, treatment with these extracellular vesicles significantly accelerated bone regeneration, as evidenced by increased bone bridging and callus formation.
CONCLUSION: These findings establish a macrophage-centric pathological network in nonunion and demonstrate that Chaenomeles speciosa-derived extracellular vesicles promote bone repair through immuno-angiogenic coupling, supporting their potential as a multi-targeted therapeutic strategy for fracture healing.
